Mr. Chairman,
I listened with a great deal of interest yesterday to the many members who took part in the discussion of the estimates of this department. There is no doubt that all members are interested in the problems of the veterans. It is not my intention to review all that was said yesterday, but there are a few comments that I wish to bring to the minister's attention, and I hope that they will be useful and that good will come out of them.
There is in my constituency one of the finest, if not the finest, veterans' hospitals in Canada. I have watched its growth from the very day when the property was acquired and the original buildings were built at the close of the first world war up until this day. I am acquainted with many of the doctors and members of the staff of the hospital, and I want to pay a word of tribute and praise to the work of the doctors, the nurses and the staff at the hospital. It is understandable that, where there are such a large number of patients in a hospital covering such a wide area, there naturally will be some complaints and perhaps some injustices, but in most cases these complaints are taken care of in a very efficient way, and I think most of the people are well satisfied with the services they are given.
While I am mentioning Westminster hospital I might say that in 1953 I also referred to the old buildings that were erected there at the close of the first world war, and the minister at that time indicated that some new buildings were proposed. Some additions have been made, and I hope the minister will indicate to the house that the rest of the old buildings will very shortly be removed and new buildings erected in their place. I should be glad if he would later indicate such to the house. I should just say, too, that I am glad that the minister and his department have taken into consideration those pensions between 40 per cent and 45 per cent. I think that action will meet with general approval. I think it is advisable to establish a plan or system of periodic reviews of all pensions and pension cases because the conditions of health change from time to time, as we all know. But there are many pensioners who hesitate to ask for a review of their particular case and there are others who do not hesitate. Sometimes there are many worthy cases that do not get the attention to which they are probably entitled.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
I speak for those pensioners who sometimes are denied a pension because their particular illness or complaint is alleged to have been attributable to causes arising before they enlisted or to post-discharge causes. I have in mind one or two of those particular cases in which it is alleged that the disability is so attributable. Yet these men served in the armed forces for several years. They were passed as being A-l, were accepted and were able to discharge their duties overseas. Yet, when they come back it is said that their disability arises because there was some illness prior to their enlistment.
There is no doubt-and this is well known to the department and to everyone here- that the earning capacity of many veterans has been reduced because of war service in one way or another. Some of them were not able to complete their education. Through disabilities some could not carry on their intended life work. The increase in the rate of pension that was granted a short time ago is still inadequate, in my opinion, in view of the inflation and the present cost of living. Also, the ceilings of earnings are too low considering living costs and the pension level.
I would just say that the grant that was given a short time ago certainly could not be considered to be extravagant. I do not think it would even be considered to be liberal.
Back in 1951 and prior to that time I mentioned in this house the suggestion that the pensions-not only those for war service but also old age pensions-should be hooked to the cost of living index. I am still of that opinion. If that were done, if you once establish what is a fair and right pension level, then as the cost of living goes up the pension would go up; and if sometime in the future the cost of living goes down, the pension could also go down. In that way the income from the pension would bear some relation to its purchasing power and there would not always be these questions arising: it being said that the pension is not high enough and that the cost of living has gone up, and then, after two or three years have elapsed, an amendment being introduced with a view to increasing the pension. This suggestion would eliminate all this problem. Also I had in my constituency four V.L.A. small holding areas, one in London township and two or three in Westminster. I am very well acquainted with the officials there, and at this point I should say that I believe they are doing a very fine job. There are very few complaints. While I am doing that, I should also pay tribute to the young veterans who have taken up these holdings. They

Supply-Veterans Affairs have taken great pride in their homes, improved their properties and they are not only taking an interest but taking part in the community in which they live, in the public life of the community through municipal affairs and church affairs. I might say that it was my privilege to have as a guest in Middlesex East the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, who addressed the veterans there some time ago. I believe that he also was greatly impressed with the community spirit and the work that they are doing.
Now, I come to the question I asked on Monday regarding the five-day 40-hour week for Westminster hospital employees and the employees of veterans hospitals in other parts of the country, who are asking that they be given the same hours of work as the employees of other departmental hospitals. I listened to the minister's explanation, and then I read the translation of his answer to the hon. member for Quebec West. While the minister has not denied to these employees the five-day 40-hour week, I think that regardless of what employment conditions may be in other industries or in other hospitals in any particular city, all the employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs should be treated similarly, whether they be in London, Halifax, Calgary or any other place. I believe it has been amply demonstrated that the employees of these hospitals can give efficient and continuous service, day and night, on the five-day 40-hour week. Consequently I am asking the minister to seriously consider the representations that have been made to him here and by the employees association last October. I ask him not to let this session go by without granting equality to all employees of the veterans hospitals across Canada.

I regret, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not seen fit at this session to introduce any legislation to improve the position of the recipients of war veterans allowance. The hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra went into this matter in considerable detail, so I am not going to take the time of the house to give reasons why action along that line should be taken. However, I would say I have never been able to understand why the government was not willing at least to raise the amount of the permissive income. For many years past I have urged, as have others, that the limit on the permissive income should be increased to at least the amount of the income tax exemptions. I would urge the government to bring in legislation at the next session to put that into effect, as well as 
to increase the actual amounts paid to recipients of war veterans allowances.
There is another matter on which perhaps I can get some information from the minister when we come to the details, but I should like to mention it at this time. I refer to the amounts paid by veterans who are not receiving disability pensions for medical attention and hospitalization. A resolution was passed by Calgary branch No. 1, my own branch of the Canadian Legion, in regard to this matter which reads as follows:
Free medical treatment for all veterans over 55 years of age with meritorious service with annual incomes in the case of single men of less than $1,800 and in the case of married men of less than $3,500.
The amount charged veterans who are not entitled to hospitalization has been increased I believe twice in the last few years, and is now in the neighbourhood of $14 per day. A married man with an income of less than $3,500 or a single man with an income of less than $1,800 finds it most difficult to pay that amount, especially when they are over 55 years of age. I should mention that they would not have to pay the full $14 per day as the amount is reduced according to income received. I submit that veterans in those income tax brackets should be given the benefits of hospitalization without payment. I should like the minister to say something about this matter of hospitalization and take under advisement the question of liberalizing the hospitalization policy in order to protect older veterans on comparatively small incomes.
I should like next to say something about the work of the imperial war graves commission. I had the opportunity last summer of seeing Canadian war cemeteries in northwestern Europe and Italy where Canadians who fought in both world wars are buried. I think I can say that without doubt they constitute the finest group of cemeteries to be found anywhere in the world. The care which they are given and the architecture which has been used to fit them into their backgrounds are of an extremely high order. I wish that every person who has a relative buried in one of those cemeteries had the opportunity to go to see it. I am glad that a grant is given to the imperial war graves commission under this department and I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to commend them upon the work they have done in maintaining the graves of our men who are buried overseas.
There is one other matter I should like to take up at this time, the question of compensation to members of the non-permanent militia, and to some extent the members of the permanent forces, when accidents occur which disable them or which result in death.

I bring this up particularly because of a case which occurred in Calgary last year. In outlining this case and referring to some of the difficulties that exist with regard to the legislation I want to make it quite clear that I am in no way reflecting upon the members of the pension commission. The chairman of the pension commission has done an outstanding job and I think he and the other members have carried on their activities with a very high sense of duty. The difficulty concerning cases of this sort, I think, primarily lies in the way the legislation reads and I think an amendment to the legislation in this regard is long overdue. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre mentioned the matter briefly yesterday and referred to the section of the act which deals with pensions to people who come under this classification. He indicated there had been considerable discussion of the matter when the estimates of this department were before the estimates committee last year but that no action had been taken concerning it. I would hope that some definite action would be taken in the near future.
The particular case I wish to give as an illustration of what happens concerns a squadron sergeant major in the South Alberta Light Horse. This man had a good record; he served overseas for five years and was awarded the military medal and he served six years in the militia. The unit is quite widely spread with one detachment at Strathmore some 40 miles from Calgary. They were in Calgary having an Armistice day celebration parade and so forth. The commanding officer of the unit got permission from western command headquarters in Edmonton to send a detachment down to take part in this anniversary day service and parade. Apparently the military transport in the form of a bus or busses had not arrived when the men gathered at the armoury in Calgary. They received a message to the effect that the bus had broken down or had been delayed in some way. The 2/IC of the regiment who was present told the men to take their own private cars. There happened to be a sufficient number of the men who had private cars to provide transportation for all of them, the presumption being that these men would eventually be reimbursed for their gasoline and expenses. In any event they proceeded to Strathmore and on the way back this particular sergeant major and another man were killed in the automobile which was driven by the other man. There was apparently no question of guilt or negligence so far as the driver was concerned and the widow of the
Supply-Veterans Affairs sergeant major was not able to take action against the driver or his estate as the result of the death of her husband.
She applied for the pension and her application was turned down at the first hearing. The decision of the commission was as follows:
Death incurred during military service in peacetime, but not pensionable under section 13 (2) as on the evidence presently available there is nothing to indicate death arose out of or was directly connected with such service.
A second hearing was held in this case and again her application was denied. I do not know whether it will be appealed but I presume it will be. The decision arises because section 13 (2) as it reads and has been interpreted makes it obligatory on the part of the person requesting the pension to prove in a case of this sort that the man was riding in a military vehicle, as I understand it, or a vehicle which had definitely been taken on strength for the time being and for which the man was being paid a mileage allowance.
In this particular case the man was on military duty and it happened through circumstances beyond his control that the military transportation did not turn up. The men were authorized by the senior officer there to use their private cars and it was in those circumstances that this man was killed. His widow's pension was denied but she would have received it if he had been killed in the military bus. It seems to me the interpretation of the act is much too narrow. The act is drawn in such a way as to cause an injustice of this sort.
I would ask the minister and the pensions commission to take this particular case under consideration again. It seems to me it might be possible by ministerial direction or by order in council that something could be done without its being necessary to change the act. I realize there probably is not time during this session to change the act but I think it would be possible by the means I have indicated to give direction to the commission to interpret this particular clause more liberally than is the case now; in other words, to interpret it in the spirit it was conceived to have when it was passed by this House of Commons. I am certain there was never any intention on the part of parliament that the widow of a man who was killed on military duty should be denied a pension because of an accident of the type I have mentioned where a military vehicle was not supplied although it was supposed to have been supplied and a private vehicle was authorized instead.
The same sort of thing applies to some extent to permanent force personnel. I was

Supply-Veterans Affairs interested in a case which had an unfavourable first and second hearing and I believe was eventually settled satisfactorily on appeal. This case involved a man who was killed overseas. Only with great difficulty was it established that he was on military duty and his widow was able to get a pension. This occurred some two or three years ago. Eventually she was able to establish the fact and was granted a pension. The circumstances were much the same as in the previous case I mentioned except that in this instance a military jeep was used. There was some difficulty in establishing that the trip it was on had been properly authorized and that the man was properly on duty, as I recall the circumstances. In any event, however, it was finally settled satisfactorily.
It seems to me that in the cases I have mentioned a little more attention should be paid to the spirit of the legislation. If this were done I believe the first case could be settled in a way that would be satisfactory to the widow and other dependents of this soldier. I certainly hope the minister will give some personal attention to this matter and will see what can be done without its being necessary to change the legislation; as I indicated before, it is perhaps too late in the session for that to be done.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to compliment the minister on the keen interest he has shown in the affairs of veterans especially during the last two or three years. I wish to thank him personally for the courtesy he has always shown me when I have brought personal cases to his attention-and this applies also to his staff in general.
I suppose I should compliment the staff because they carry out the letter of the law, but at the same time I also complain that the letter of the law is predominant in the administration of the veterans legislation and I think the spirit of the law and not the legal interpretation should prevail. It is on that subject that I wish to say a few words at this time.
In order to overcome the difficulty I have mentioned it seems to me a little more leeway should be given to the local administrators, those people who know the local problems and the persons involved. They are far more conversant with the individual cases and are better equipped to find solutions to the various problems than is someone in Ottawa or possibly in Vancouver or Calgary. I think that if a little more power were given to them to interpret the law according to the spirit of the act, many of the problems about which we are now worrying would be solved.
[Mr. Harkness.l

In many instances cases which are recommended to be dealt with in a certain way by local officials who know the circumstances have been turned down by senior administrators who have given a narrow interpretation to the wording of the act. The justice of the case did not enter into it, the morality of the case did not enter into it, the spirit of the case did not enter into it; there was simply a pure, logical reasoning as to the legality of the act.
I was a member of the veterans committee when it sat and I know the attention that was given to any question that came up. I know the feeling of all hon. members that the veteran should be given the benefit of any doubt, yet in practice this is not always done. I could outline the details quite quickly, but I shall not do so at this time. This is my main reason for advocating the setting up of a permanent veterans committee. I think it would be a far more important committee than many of those that now go on year after year, sometimes going through a session without meeting. Such a committee would carry out most important functions of great value to the minister and to the veterans.
Without such a committee we are in danger of gradually building up a legal bureaucracy, a group without a heart, a legal entity ready to carry out only, the letter of the law. If we had a veterans committee dealing with cases, that atmosphere would be changed when a veteran had to appear before a board or other group. I am sure that neither parliament nor the people of Canada wish this condition to continue.
It is true that we have made progress equal to that made in any other country, but there are many problems still unsolved affecting the veteran. I would mention those veterans who served in England during the first world war. Their number is getting smaller each year but they are still denied the right of pension. The hon. member for Kootenay West referred yesterday to two men who had joined up and who served as clerks, one in England and one in France. The one man is receiving a pension while the other is denied a pension. Such discrepancies should be removed and all veterans treated on a fair basis.
I still think that we should make the permissive income under the War Veterans Allowance Act more in keeping with the cost of living today, and the widows of veterans who have resided in Canada for some years should be recognized as being pensionable. I shall not go into the details of these cases, as the minister knows them better than I do.

Another problem which could be dealt with by a committee sitting year after year is one such as has cropped up recently in British Columbia, and this may be true also of other parts of Canada. British Columbia has recently made a reassessment of properties for school tax purposes. I have here a resolution which I should like to place on the record so the minister may know what I am talking about. It reads:
Whereas the reassessment of property in British Columbia which has recently taken place, grave concern is felt for veterans occupying small holdings under the Veterans Land Act, having their holdings of one acre, reclassified from agricultural into residential districts resulting in an increased assessment of at least double the original amount and a good chance of increased taxes due to present tendency of real estate speculation, which surround the V.L.A. project. This particularly' applies to about 60 veterans located in the BankHead district near Kelowna, B.C. These veterans were rehabilitated on these acre lots with a view of their being able to supplement their earnings, now the reassessment will defeat the government's original intention and following the pattern of the first world war veteran, will force the veteran to vacate his holding as was the case of very many of our older veterans, who had taken up land under the Soldier Settlement Land Act and who were forced to quit, because of economic conditions.
Therefore, be it resolved that this north Okanagan zone request the provincial command to make strong representations to the provincial government protesting the reassessment of V.L.A. small holdings into residential areas and thus enable them to derive the benefit which has been granted to them under the veterans charter.
I appreciate that this is probably a provincial problem, but nevertheless the Department of Veterans Affairs has a responsibility to look after the interests of these veterans. In my opinion the least they can do is to protest to the provincial or municipal authorities this reassessment-in this case it is the province-on the ground that the veteran is entitled to special benefits. These men went on these small holdings with the understanding that benefits would accrue to them as long as they occupied the land.
The hon. member for Calgary North referred to the problem of the man who is killed while technically not on duty. Whether or not a man is on duty, I submit he is still a soldier. One or two cases have occurred recently in my riding. A young fellow who had served three years in Germany took a ride in a civilian car and was killed. This case is similar to the one mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North. This man leaves a widow and two children and so far they have not received a cent from any department of government. They cannot qualify under this act; they cannot qualify under the army or in any other way that I can find out.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
It seems to me that any man who joins the forces should be granted protection at all times for accident and death in order that the widow and orphans he may leave behind shall be protected. In this case the widow and the two orphans are living on charity. It seems to me that every soldier on joining the forces should be given the protection of an insurance policy to cover everything that may happen, with provision for the payment of at least $20,000 to his widow and family in the event of his death. There is a moral obligation to protect these young men in every way. They are depending entirely upon the army for their income and the welfare of their families should be protected.
We have not met this particular problem. I do not blame the department for this, but I hope the department will co-operate with the Department of National Defence in an effort to find a solution something like that mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North so that in future we will not be faced with cases of this kind.
Another problem concerns the farmer settler. I am not going to go into detail about this matter because I have already written to the minister and he has kindly promised to look into it. Last year several farmers in the Cawston area of British Columbia suffered severe frost damage to their young orchards. Somebody suggested that possibly some legislative enactment might be made whereby pensions would be attached to the cost of living index. I believe that objective would be rather difficult to attain. However, I believe this. In consequence of a continuing rise in the cost of living and also in the expansion of monetary instability having regard to purchasing power, I believe we can take it for granted that the present level of prices is a plateau from which we will not expect any retrogression in the days ahead. If that be so, then having regard to the purchasing power of money, I believe there will have to come at an early date a reconsideration of the Pension Act in so far as the amount of pension is concerned, to the end that the standards of living of those who served will not be reduced.
I should now like to say a word or two with reference to a matter that has been discussed on previous occasions, namely, war veterans allowances. As the situation is at the present time, the ceiling on income for single veterans is $840 and for married veterans $1,440. I find it hard to understand why the amount should not be increased to the level of that amount which, under the Income Tax Act, becomes exempt from income taxation. This question has been asked the minister before: where is the sense of fairness in this situation? Everyone is entitled to the old age pension, whether it is the Prime Minister who receives it or somebody else. Every citizen in our country is entitled to it at 70 years of age. Why should those in receipt of war veterans allowance find the amount of their old age pensions in effect reduced on the achievement of the age of 70 years? That is something that one hears universally complained about. It is something that is unjust for, by reason of the present ceilings, it places those who served and their dependents in a second-class position with respect to others who did not serve. It brings about a state of affairs that is unfair and unjust and it constitutes a discrimination that cannot be justified. I ask the minister once more-as he has been asked on previous occasions

I regret, as have other members before me, that the minister has to be the Minister of Veterans Affairs and at the same time the Postmaster General. He demonstrated a unique ability to grasp, within a short period of time, the many details attached to the office of Postmaster General. I think it was remarkable, considering the way he had this additional burden put on him, that he was able to display such a unique ability to understand the workings of that other department of government, a major department. However, I think it is imposing an undue burden on the minister. No man, no matter how able he may be, is able to administer, in the degree that is expected of him, the department that he now holds as well as another department. I hope the day is not too far away when the Minister of Veterans Affairs will again be only the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I am sure the minister is also looking forward to the day when he can shed his additional responsibilities. However, I hope that the view expressed in this house sometime ago will not be realized. I hope the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will not be saddled with the Post Office Department. If there is any minister who has shown his inadequacy in this house it has been the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and the Post Office Department is one of the last departments for which I would like to see him made responsible.
We are not supposed to mention the details of the minister's department at this time and I do not intend to do so. I intend to confine myself to the generalities of his department. When I look at the net earnings of Canadian corporations for the first three months of this year and realize they are in excess of $750 million, and when I look at the estimates of this department and see that the minister is asking for approximately $250 million, I think I can fairly say the needs of the returned men of Canada are very modest indeed. My only regret is that the government is unwilling to grant in their entirety

the requests of the Canadian Legion. After all, these men were willing to sacrifice all in defence of democracy.
The Liberal party was not willing to sacrifice all in defence of democracy. I well remember that when the last war was at its height the C.C.F. party was advocating that we risk all in defence of democracy including not only the lives of these men but also the possessions of the people of Canada. However, the Liberal party saw fit at that time to risk only the lives of Canadian citizens. The time has come for us to pay tribute to those who risked all at that time.
I see that we are prepared to spend 5 per cent of the income of this government in order to help those who were willing to risk all. We are prepared to spend 40 per cent of our income on possible future wars. The Department of National Defence is asking for 40 cents out of our dollar whereas the Department of Veterans Affairs is asking for only 5 cents out of our dollar. I feel the balance is rather out of line, Mr. Chairman. I feel that if we want the Canadian people to be sincere in their effort in any future war-and I hope it will not occur- the relationship of the 5 per cent and 40 per cent will have to be brought into line. The government of Canada and our economy generally can well afford to grant the demands of the Canadian Legion which always have been modest and reasonable.
I can understand some of the hesitancy on the part of the government to grant a larger measure of welfare to our veterans when I think of the attitude of the government to the cause of democracy. These people-most of them at least-were willing to sacrifice their lives for our way of life and for our system of government which is exemplified by the parliament of Canada, and yet the Liberal party has been able to accomplish what Kaiser Wilhelm and Adolf Hitler were unable to accomplish. The Kaiser of Germany went all out to destroy democracy and Adolf Hitler made a supreme effort to rid the world of democracy and yet the Liberal government through actions recently displayed revealed that it was able to accomplish what the Kaiser and Adolf Hitler were unable to accomplish, the destruction of parliamentary democracy in this country.
There were hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens who were willing to lay down their lives for the sake of parliamentary democracy. May I remind the house that Hitler also had a parliament where the majority ruled, Mussolini had a parliament where the majority ruled and I understand that in Moscow there are approximately 1,600 members in their parliament where the
Supply-Veterans Affairs majority also* rules. We had hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens who were willing to sacrifice their lives and say they would die if necessary for our own British system of government and yet this government utilized the lives of Canadians in a cause that I have reason to suspect was most insincere. I have reason to think the government was more concerned about the welfare of the profit-making institutions who would make money on war than the lives of Canadians who were willing to die for a cause they thought was the cause of freedom but which has now been decidedly proven to have been the interest of the Liberal party of Canada alone.
I return to the point concerning which I am supposed to speak at this time. In the over-all picture the veterans' interests are insignificant in the eyes of the Liberal party of Canada. The interests of parliament and of democracy are insignificant. The interests of the Liberal party and the so-called overwhelming majority in the House of Commons-although not in the nation as a whole *-have to take second place to the Liberal party itself.

As I said before, the army benevolent fund is in a different situation. As I understand it, the purpose of that fund is to give grants, loans and other benefits to veterans who served in the army during the war. The army has a separate army welfare fund to look after servicemen who are presently serving, while in the case of the air force the one fund looks after both classes of men.
We have a situation where a fund is not responsible directly to parliament, yet is receiving certain benefits from public moneys, even though indirectly. This is something which bears a close relationship to problems which arise in the Department of Veterans Affairs, and I think there should be a closer contact between these two funds. I should like to think that the minister or his parliamentary assistant, who may be more directly interested in this, would look carefully into this situation.
As the minister knows, during the war large sums of money accumulated in the nonpublic funds accounts in messes and canteens of the air force, and toward the end of the war these were turned over to the air force benevolent fund. Contributions continue to be made to that fund from similar sources in the air force. There is a strong feeling growing up among veterans who served in the air force that they do not have the same opportunity of benefiting from the air force benevolent fund as do the men who are presently serving. In the case of a man presently serving there are officers immediately at hand who are well acquainted with the benefits which are available and applications can be made and recommendations sent forward if the case is a good one, and a grant or loan is usually made. The air force veteran

who is now a civilian feels that he is denied the services of such qualified men, that therefore his case is not so well presented, and as a result the benefits which he receives are not in proportion to the contributions which veterans as a group made during the war.
I think the system adopted in the case of the army benevolent fund is a good one. In that case field services are provided by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I would recommend that the minister look carefully into the situation with regard to the air force benevolent fund to see if a similar arrangement could not be made. I think it is most important that it should be made in the case of the air force, because the proportion of men now serving in the air force as compared with those who served during the war is much greater than in the case of the army. Therefore it is more important, not less, that two separate funds should be set up; an air force welfare fund for serving members of that service, and an air force benevolent fund which would apply only to veterans of the air force.
After all, it was the veterans who in the first case contributed through their nonpublic fund accounts very large amounts of money to the benevolent fund. Toward the end of the war they lost complete control of that as individuals. The non-public funds were turned over to the air force benevolent fund, and in most cases canteens, messes and so on had no alternative but to turn over the profits that had accumulated during the war. I know from experience that in many cases messes operated at a higher profit than they would have if they had anticipated what was going to happen.
It may be said that I have just expressed an opinion or that several veterans of the air force, who tend to grouse anyway, are just complaining because they do not feel they are getting a fair break, but I see a paragraph in the eleventh annual report of the Royal Canadian Air Force benevolent fund which substantiates what I have to say. They condemn themselves with their own words, in my way of thinking, in this regard. Please do not misunderstand me. Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure the hon. member for Calgary North that, in my remarks addressed to the hon. member for Prince Albert, I was not questioning for one minute the accuracy of the facts which he stated to this house, but simply questioning whether those facts had been properly put before the commission.
I should like, at the beginning of my remarks, to thank all hon. members who have participated in this debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. As is usual and proper, there have been praises for the officials of the department and criticism of the minister and of the policy of the government, and I suppose that is as it should be. However, I might say that I readily accept on behalf of the officials of my department the praises which were expressed of them, because I feel that the veterans' charter is administered and implemented not only with efficiency but in a humanitarian and understanding way. That is done both at headquarters and in the field by officers of the department who are veterans themselves in almost all cases, and I think that might be an explanation of their attitude of mind.
I must say I was particularly glad to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South emphasize the fact that the department does act, that it does things without any special urging or pressure, because as I said in my opening remarks and have said on other


occasions, it is the aim of the government, and it is certainly the aim of the Department of Veterans Affairs, to keep the veterans' charter constantly under review to ensure that it is always up to date and that it is meeting as much as possible the changing needs of veterans and their dependents.
I do not propose to deal at this stage with all the points that have been raised. I think I can do so better on the specific votes as they are called. I think it will be agreed that most of the points raised by way of criticism are matters that have been discussed before in the house, outside the house and before the special committee on veterans affairs. I think that all hon. members will agree that in many instances it is most difficult to draw the line for qualification for benefits under legislation such as that which comprises the veterans' charter. It is difficult, whether the line be one regarding a means test, or service qualification, or one concerning a time limit. In acts such as the War Veterans Allowance Act, the Pension Act and the Veterans' Land Act, no matter where the line is drawn there will always be borderline ones which just fail to qualify and may in fact well be cases of hardship. I think that is true of all legislation of a social character, what might be termed social legislation. It is one of the difficulties that governments meet, whether at the federal, provincial or municipal level.
Most of the hon. members who have spoken up to now on this item have referred at length to the ceilings on permissible income in the War Veterans Allowance Act. I think in the debate on second reading of the bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act last session I submitted at quite some length and to the best of my ability the reasoning of the government in fixing the ceilings at their present levels, that is $840 for a single man and $1,440 for a recipient at the married rate. I pointed out, at the time, that if the ceilings had been established at $1,200 single and $2,000 married, the War Veterans Allowance Act could and would, in a number of cases, be a supplement to normal income.
I also pointed out the necessity of keeping all benefits available to veterans in balance, and that when fixing the ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act cognizance must be taken of the disability pensioner under the Pension Act. I also pointed out that this had always been done throughout the history of veterans' legislation in this country. The present ceiling of $70 a month for a single recipient is equivalent to slightly more than a 55 per cent disability pension, that is, a pension paid for injury incurred in service,

while the ceiling of $120 a month for a married recipient is equivalent to approximately a 70 per cent pension under the Pension Act.
As I said at that time, if the ceiling on the single rate were raised to $1,200 that would be the equivalent of an 80 per cent disability pension. It would be in fact $25 less a month than a 100 per cent disability pension. A ceiling of $2,000 on permissible income at the married rate would be just $40 a year less than a 100 per cent disability pension at married rate. A 100 per cent disability married pensioner gets $2,040 or $170 a month.
The hon. member for Royal said that a disability pensioner with a small pension or a small superannuation allowance is prejudiced because of these permissible ceilings. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that, regardless of where you set the ceiling, a case could be made showing that the ceiling was not fair to certain people. That is what I was pointing out in the earlier part of my remarks when I referred to the difficulties that exist in dealing with such legislation.
For instance, let us say that the ceiling was raised to $1,200 a year for a single man. A war veterans allowance recipient at age 70 would receive $40 by way of old age security payment and $60 war veterans allowance, or the maximum permitted under this $1,200 ceiling. But let us consider the case of a 45 per cent disability pensioner under such circumstances. That the case, for instance, of a man who has lost an eye. I believe that, according to the table of disabilities, the loss of one eye creates a right to a 40 per cent disability pension. Let us say this man is a 45 per cent pensioner, that he has lost one eye and has some gunshot wounds. At age 70 this man would receive $675 under the Pension Act, he would receive $480 under the Old Age Security Act and roughly about $5 a month by way of war veterans allowance, making in all a total of $1,200. I think that this 45 per cent disability pensioner might say, to use the terminology of the hon. member for Royal, that he was prejudiced in that he would be getting very little benefit from his disability pension.
I dealt at much greater length with this question last year and I did note that although hon. members have again made the same representations-I know they do so with the greatest sincerity-no one dealt with the side of the case that I put up last year.
In the course of his remarks one hon. member said this: "It would not cost the government very much more just to raise the ceiling to $1,200 for the single recipient and $2,000 for the married recipient." I wish that were so, Mr. Chairman. However, it 67509-375i

Then, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Royal asked me if the war veterans allowance recipients reaching the age of 70 would not be able to benefit by the full amount of the old age security payment if the ceilings were raised to the levels that have been

suggested. Well, that is quite true. This matter was raised by other members. On other occasions, I have given the government's view on the matter. I know I have been questioned in this house and outside. The tact of the matter is, whether or not one wishes to admit it, that one has to go back some years to the origin of the war veterans allowance to realize just what was behind that legislation. I have said this before the Canadian Legion at their dominion convention, and nobody contradicted me. Nobody has contradicted me so far. I should like, if I may, to quote exactly what I did say at that time, because it explains why certain things that are requested under the War Veterans Allowance Act, in the view of the government cannot be done. These remarks were made in 1954 at Toronto:
War veterans allowances have been based, since their inception in 1930, on the premise that service in a theatre of war preaged a veteran and placed him in a more unfavourable position in the labour market than would have been the case if he had not had such service. Because of this accelerated aging, the allowances were introduced to provide for veterans who needed at age 60, a form of social security not available to their non-veteran contemporaries until they reached the age of 70.
In effect, it was an old age security scheme designed especially to meet conditions peculiar to veterans who had seen combat service.
Now-some of you may object to that assimilation of the war veterans allowance to other social security measures. But the fact remains that a perusal of the debates in the house and the deliberations of the parliamentary committee of 1930 will bear me out on this point.
This being the case, any major changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act-particularly some which have been suggested-cannot help but have serious financial implications in other fields of governmental activities.
Mr. Chairman, that basically is why, when a recipient of war veterans allowance reaches the age of 70, the amount of his allowance is reduced by the amount of the old age security payment he receives. Unfortunately that is the position and no one has ever denied it. It is impossible to do so if you go back and study the origin of the legislation and the debates that took place at that time.

I do not fully agree with the hon. member for Royal, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the dual service veteran. I think the hon. member is as familiar as I am with the history of that particular section of the War Veterans Allowance Act. This change was brought in originally in 1944, and it was an order in council passed under the authority of the War Measures Act. It was known as the "veterans' dual service pension order". The hon. member will recall that, when we sat in the veterans affairs committee in the years that followed the war and were asked to put in statutory form the various orders that had been passed, something had to be done about that particular pension order and it was added to the War Veterans Allowance Act at that time as part III of the act.
Finally when we reviewed and consolidated the act in 1952-my hon. friend sat as a member of that committee-it was decided that rather than have a separate part of the War Veterans Allowance Act to deal with


the dual service pension order, it would be simply included in the act as a section and it became, I think, section 30. These veterans were described in section 30 of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I say we cannot overlook the fact that the war veterans allowance was originally created and has always been looked upon as legislation designed to deal with the needy veteran who served in an actual theatre of war. It has been said that many of these men stayed in England not because of their own choice. They may have been kept there because they were cn the administrative staff or for some other reason, and mention has been made of the fact that they would have liked to serve in an actual theatre of war. I point out, Mr. Chairman, that is the case with every man who enlists. If service in England during world war I is recognized as a qualification for war veterans allowance I do not see how we could eventually avoid recognizing service in Canada.

My hon. friend is quite an expert on figures and the interpretation of statistics, but I can only give to the committee the views which my officials and the financial members of my staff give to me. Those are based on our past experience with other veterans.
There is another point which was mentioned by some hon. members and to which I should like to refer briefly. This concerns the payment of war veterans allowance to recipients who were living outside of Canada for reasons of health. Last year the hon. member for Kootenay West spoke at some length on this subject and I told him that we
Supply-Veterans Affairs would be looking into these particular cases, which would call for an amendment to the act. Since that time I have had discussions with officials of my department, and I asked them to investigate this situation thoroughly.
I regret to say that, after a great deal of discussion and thought we find it is not feasible to amend section 14 (1) as was suggested. Under the present legislation a recipient may absent himself from Canada for a period of up to three months in any calendar year without affecting the payment of his war veterans allowance, and he may dovetail his stay outside of Canada from one calendar year into another and thus be able to absent himself for six months without having his allowance reduced. However, he can do this only once every two years.
There are serious obstacles to making the suggested change in the legislation, one being the provision of treatment for recipients of war veterans allowance who are living outside of Canada. A great proportion of them need medical treatment from time to time, and this would involve the extension of the provisions of section 12 of the veterans' treatment regulations. It would be most difficult indeed to implement such provisions.
Then there would be the difficulty of arranging for periodical medical examinations of veterans who have not reached the age of 60 years but who are in receipt of war veterans allowance because they are totally unemployable. Such examinations would be most difficult indeed under the circumstances. There would also be the matter of administering the means test in connection with people living outside of Canada. Of course if we followed the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and eliminated the means test that obstacle would disappear, but I am afraid I cannot agree to that suggestion.
Complicated administrative problems would be created where the wife of a recipient of war veterans allowance did not accompany him when he left Canada but remained in Canada. It would be most difficult to amend this section of the act to permit a war veterans allowance recipient to go outside Canada to only one or two specific countries. During the course of the debate last year reference was made to the veteran who might wish to go to the southern part of the United States or Mexico. If the act were opened up to permit the payment of allowances in other parts of the world, the administrative problems thus created would be most complicated.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned the specific case of a veteran who wanted to go to Mexico. Frankly I do not

Supply-Veterans Affairs know how we could deal administratively with veterans in that country. As I understand it, the facilities for looking after veterans in that country certainly are not such as would meet the necessities created by our act. For that reason we have not found it feasible to agree to this change at this time.
I realize that I have taken longer than I had intended. There are many other matters on which I wish to answer hon. members, but I suggest that possibly it would be more useful to deal with specific items as they come up.

It raises a problem on which I should like the minister to make a brief statement. We know that the war veterans allowance is paid under various categories, over 60 and so on and so forth, permanently unemployable, and then you come down to one who, because of physical or mental disability or insufficiency combined with economic handicaps, is incapable of maintaining himself.
The situation which was brought rather forcibly to my mind this morning by a rather pathetic letter-a situation with which the minister or his departmental officials dealt two years ago and which has now been revised-is one such as this. You have a veteran who has been receiving war veterans allowance. He had a kidney disability, as a result of which one kidney was removed by operation. He had tuberculosis of the other. He had been receiving war veterans allowance up to two years ago, when somebody decided that he was then capable of earning a living. An appeal was taken and as a result the war veterans allowance was restored. Since then he has had two more operations on that kidney, so his condition apparently was not too good two years ago. Now he has been in Camp Hill hospital for examination, and he received a letter last week saying that, according to the doctors, he was now capable of earning a living. So his war veterans allowance has been cancelled as of July 31 this year.
I can understand the position of the department. Apparently, the section is mandatory and provides that if the medical officer says that he is capable of earning a living, there is no alternative. Frankly, I do not know what the minister can do about it. I think there should be some elasticity brought into the picture somewhere. Obviously there has been such elasticity or else he could not have got around the appeal two years ago. When you go on to the next section, you find that it is much more elastic, where provision is made for payment of benefits to employable veterans because there the requirement is that he is unable to maintain himself or is capable of taking only light employment.

The situation is this. This particular man is a labourer with a grade VI education and living away out in the country. I know he was told at one time, "Perhaps you can operate an elevator". May I also point out the other difference that would still obtain between the war veterans allowance recipient, if the ceiling were set at $1,200, and the disability pensioner, namely that there is no ceiling on the income of a disability pensioner. It seems to me that these same answers apply to the other examples the minister gave, and that in fact to establish a higher ceiling on war veterans allowances would not be as unfair-I am not sure if that is the word he used but that is the spirit I caught from what he said-as he suggested it would be to the disability pensioner. I do not hear any disability pensioners complaining about the suggestion that something better be done for war veterans allowance recipients. As a matter of fact those ceilings in the War Veterans Allowance Act have a limiting effect on the income of many recipients of the disability pension.

As the minister and all of us know, where a disability pensioner is receiving an amount as a disability pension which is equal to or higher than the ceiling set in the War Veterans Allowance Act he is denied the possibility of any supplement under the War Veterans Allowance Act. On the other hand, if the ceiling were raised under the War Veterans Allowance Act it would be of assistance not only to those who receive only the war veterans allowance, not only to the others who might come in, but it would be of assistance as well to many who receive disability pensions in the lower percentage brackets.
The minister also gave the example of a war veterans allowance recipient now drawing $60 a month. He said that if the ceiling were raised to $1,200 a year or $100 a month, that would permit him, when he reached 70 years of age, to draw the $40 old age pension in full and still keep the full amount of his war veterans allowance, bringing him up to $100 per month. Against that the minister set the case of a 45 per cent disability pensioner drawing $675 a year disability pension and $480 old age security or a total of $1,155 a year. He said further that that person, if the ceiling were raised to $1,200, would be able to draw only another $45 a year as war veterans allowance.
As I took it from the minister, he seemed to suggest that there was something of an imbalance between the treatment accorded the disability pensioner and the war veterans allowance recipient in that situation. May I point out that so far as the war veterans allowance recipient to whom he referred is concerned, prior to reaching age 70, at $60 a month he is already receiving $720 a year which, of course, is more than the 45 per cent disability pensioner is receiving under that legislation. The 45 per cent disability pensioner does not complain about that so long as there is a margin that permits him to get a supplement by way of war veterans allowance if his income is not adequate.
All told, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that these comparisons the minister sought to make between the position of the disability pensioner and the war veterans allowance recipient are not valid. For these, and for the other excellent reasons that have been advanced in the discussion of these estimates, I hope that further consideration will be given by the government to raising these ceilings. I wish the government would start making some upward move at this session. Certainly the ceilings should be set at nothing less than the figures suggested by the Legion of $1,200 single or $2,000 married, but surely it is possible to make a start in that upward direction at this session.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

subtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER

I wish to support the request of the Canadian Legion that the allowable income ceilings on war veterans allowance recipients be increased. I think over the years the Canadian Legion have taken a very responsible attitude so far as government legislation is concerned. Their proposals have always been moderate and responsible. I think their proposals today in relation to the war veterans allowance are very modest indeed. They are not asking, though I think they might have reason to ask, that the basic pension itself be increased above the $60 for a single person or $108 for a married couple. The new income ceiling they suggest of $1,200 per year single or $2,000 a year for a person who is married I think is quite low enough.
Today the cost of living is at an all-time high. If such a person could obtain the extra allowable income to reach the $100 a month, that would be little enough to meet the current cost of living. The Legion is asking for only a $30 per month increase for a single person and $46.66 increase in the allowable income per month for married veterans.
I would like to see, as others have said, a veterans affairs committee established again. I believe that in the past members of that committee have taken a very sympathetic attitude towards the veterans. I believe that if a representative committee of this house were to discuss this question they would bring in a recommendation that would, in large measure, meet the requests of the Canadian Legion.
I have only a few more remarks to make, Mr. Chairman.

The hon. member for Royal is not able to be here this evening because of the activities of the research committee, and he asked me to bring up the matter of assistance provided under the war veterans allowance. I note that the amount spent under this vote last year was about $375,000 less than the amount voted. The act provides for fhe payment of $10 per month or $120 per year to completely unemployable old veterans who are receiving war veterans assistance, but it would appear that the average payment is considerably under that amount. I should like to know the average amount paid to these unemployable old veterans. My information is that instead of $120 per year being paid the average is between $60 and $70, or about one-half.
It would appear from the fact that the amount voted last year was considerably underspent that the regulations have been rigorously applied. I submit that this is one group who are probably in about as bad a situation as any group in the Dominion of Canada. These old veterans are completely unemployable and it is impossible for them to supplement their war veterans allowances. In spite of that fact, if my information is correct on the average they get only a little more than half what the legislation provides.
I should like the minister to tell us what was the average amount paid and why the vote was underspent by more than one-third last year?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member will remember that last year we amended the act to increase the ceilings and the rates, and in so doing we brought in additional veterans. It turned out that we had overestimated the number who might qualify for assistance from the fund. Furthermore, by raising the rates some people who might have applied for assistance under the fund did not do so.
In making our estimate this year we went by our experience last year, but from what has happened in April, May and June it would appear that we may have underestimated. As compared with the same months last year the number of applications received in April, May and June this year were 40 per cent higher.
As of March 31, 1956, there were 6,256 recipients who were receiving assistance

from the fund, and of that number 3,070 represented new applications made during the year, the balance being carried over from the previous year. Of the 2,072 veterans receiving allowances on the basis of married rates, 1,574 received $10 per month or more. Out of a total of 272 widows, 232 received $10 per month or more. Of those two groups, 311 received single payments averaging $58 per year.
In the case of those on single rates, out of 1,501 veterans, 756 received $8 per month or more; out of 1,467 widows, 1,158 received $8 per month or more. In that group 560 received average single payments of $42. Out of a total of 2,348 married rate recipients, 2,117 received assistance at the rate of 85 per cent or more. Out of 2,968 recipients, 2,474 received assistance at the rate of 80 per cent or more.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A rapid bit of mental arithmetic would indicate that the figures the minister has given indicate that the average payment was around $7 per month instead of $10. It would seem to me that as the amount involved here is almost negligible considering our general revenues, being $100,000 or something less than that, this is a case where the legislation and the regulations should be applied in the most liberal manner possible.
I see the minister nodding his head in agreement. I hope that in future years these people will be given the maximum amount the law allows, the $10 per month, without too much question being asked; because, as I say, the total amount of money involved is very small. For people who are getting say $60 per month total income plus the amount of this allowance, if they get $10 per month perhaps they can just get by, whereas if they get only $66 or $67 per month it may mean a terrific amount of hardship. It is a question of people on an extraordinarily low total income where every dollar makes a great deal of difference as to whether they merely exist or perhaps exist with one, two or three of the simple pleasures of life.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think the hon. member will recall that in my opening statement I did mention that, basing ourselves on last year's experience, although the formula used for the assistance fund had been broadened last year, there were cases where we did not think it met the problem, and members of my department were looking into this to try to find a solution to those problems.

Supply-Veterans Affairs and war veterans' assistance? Is there any agreement between the two departments as to which will look after the borderline cases? speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

The problem has not arisen as yet, and I can assure my hon. friend that we shall study this situation.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: What worries me about this is the fact that it could be quite convenient for the Department of Veterans Affairs to disclaim any responsibility in many of these cases and put the onus on the unemployment assistance act, under which the cost would be shared by the provincial government.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: At the present time, payments for unemployment under the Unemployment Insurance Act are considered as income under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and they have to be taken into consideration when computing the permissible income of the recipient of war veterans allowance. I should think that principle would apply to the new act but, as I said, the matter has not been studied as yet.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is not exactly a parallel comparison, because the new act, the unemployment assistance act, is drawn up in such a way as to supplement the Unemployment Insurance Act; and there would not be much overlap between the Unemployment Insurance Act and the war veterans allowance or assistance, but there might be between the unemployment assistance and the war veterans allowance. It appears to me that there might possibly be a tendency to take many of these borderline cases who are applying for war veterans allowance or war veterans assistance and place them under the unemployment assistance act, in which case the province would be responsible for carrying a part of the burden.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It will be looked into, but I might say that in the past the situation has been that where there are borderline cases we get them under the war veterans allowance.

speechtext: Could the minister say who administers the benevolent fund and just what veterans benefit under that fund?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

The army benevolent fund, as my hon. friend knows, is set up under statute. It is administered by a board headed by General Murchie. The members of that board are: Lieutenant General Murchie, chairman; Brigadier Gauvreau, Montreal; Captain Peck, Vancouver; Lieutenant General San-som, of Fredericton, I believe, but representing the Canadian Legion; and Major Wickens, representing the national council of veterans' associations. subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: What kind of cases would be looked after?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: They are all world war II veterans who can benefit from the fund, because it was made up of regimental funds, mess funds and so on accumulated in the second world war. They will endeavour as much as possible to help in the rehabilitation of veterans and in meeting major emergencies with which the veteran cannot cope because of the high financial cost that might be involved. They will also help in re-establishing a veteran who is in bad financial circumstances by advancing money, possibly getting agreement among his creditors to accept certain sums, and set him back on his feet.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

How many of those formerly pensioned are now deceased? My third question is this. How many of those at present living have had increases in their pensions? While it may not apply directly to the Department of Veterans Affairs, nevertheless I think some information could be derived which would be useful.
I refer to coronary disease. I am aware that coronary disease is not regarded as pensionable by the Canadian pension commission or by the British commission, though I think there is a pension for aggravation. If this information that I am trying to bring out were available, I think it should be made available to the medical people in general. When you have the situation of a man who served five years overseas and proved his mettle by winning the Military Medal; who served six years in the militia and had an extraordinarily good record; who obeyed the orders of his commanding officer to turn out on a parade and who, as a result of turning out on the parade, lost his life; and when really because of a technicality based on a mischance when he lost his life his widow has been turned down for pension, I think you have a situation which calls into question in the minds of a large number of people the claims which we have heard that our veterans' legislation is

the best in the world. It also discourages people from joining the militia or continuing in the militia.
It seems to me it is just not good enough to leave the situation as it is. This one case which I have mentioned happens to illustrate the matter particularly well, but there have been other cases of the same kind. It is not good enough to leave the situation where it stands. I think the minister owes it to his own department and to the defence department as well as to this house to make some kind of statement in regard to this particular section 13 (2), I believe it is, of the Pension Act, as to what can be done in order to correct what I think is a very unfortunate state of affairs in regard to this particular case as well as cases generally along this line.

The difficulty is, as I said, that the decision has been made really on a technicality. It was founded on a mischance. Supply-Veterans Affairs
In other words, as I say, it is a technicality based on a mischance. subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is the section 13, subsection 2 which has been causing so much difficulty for a number of years. The answer the minister gives is that the pension commission is an independent body. We accept that. When an inquiry is made of the pension commission they say they have to conduct their proceedings and make their decisions in accordance with the act. The act can be changed only by parliament, and the person who should introduce such a change is the minister. Last year in the estimates committee he told us that this section 13 subsection 2 was under consideration. He has now reported that it has been considered and he sees no way in which it can be altered.
The hon. member for Calgary North has raised now a very good example of the weakness of the act as it is interpreted by the pension commission. It is only about four years ago that I raised in this house a somewhat similar case affecting a member of the regular forces who lost his life. Again it was section 13, subsection 2 under which the decision was rendered. When the hon. member for Calgary North was talking about this particular instance, naturally my mind went back to the McAulay case that I raised before the appeal board of the pension commission and spoke about in the House of Commons. The people who suffer under these decisions which the pension commission finds it has to make in accordance with the act are the widows and children. Surely that is not the intention of parliament or the Canadian people.
In both these instances, the one raised by the hon. member for Calgary North and the one I raised four years ago, the men had given first class service overseas. In the case to which I referred the man continued in the regular army back home, and in the case referred to by the hon. member for Calgary North the man continued in the militia. Both men gave continuous service in the interests of the Canadian armed forces. In both cases the widows are now left without assistance; in both cases the men were acting under orders, as we see it, and both the hon. member for Calgary North and I have had some


military experience. In both cases the pension commission found that these accidents were not directly connected with military service. It just does not make sense to us.
I recall in the McAulay case I was informed by a member of the pension commission that the corporal who later was killed should have refused to obey the order of the sergeant who put in his possession the jeep which he drove. When the hon. member for Prince Albert was talking about the Hepworth case that was mentioned earlier I thought the answer might have been given by some member of the commission to the effect that the men should have refused to obey the order of the major, the second in command of the battalion; that they should have said to him, "Sir, we cannot travel to our destination in civilian cars because if we do that we will not be obeying the rules and regulations".
Subordinate ranks simply cannot take stands like that. They have to obey orders, whether the order is given by a sergeant to a corporal, by a major to a lieutenant or by men of other ranks. To people who have served it is just nonsense to suggest that junior ranks can resist orders given by people senior to them.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that section 13(2) will have to be reconsidered by the minister. As the hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned, the Department of Justice might very well be called in to give some advice on the matter, which is becoming a serious problem.
Last year in the estimates committee I asked the chairman of the pensions commission for some figures with regard to the number of applications to the pension commission by former members of the regular forces under section 13(2). He gave figures for a 5-year period from January, 1950, to March, 1955, and these appear at page 578 of the proceedings of the special committee on estimates of last year. In that 5-year period 6,952 cases came before the commission either on first or second hearing or on appeal, and 89 per cent were rejected. That is a very high rejection figure, and all those rejections were under section 13(2).
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that much more serious consideration must be given to this matter. It is intolerable that the burden of these accidental deaths should fall upon the completely innocent widows and children. It must be remembered that the wives permit their husbands to take part in these military activities, and the army and other service authorities urge the married women to permit their husbands to spend two or three nights a week in militia training of this sort. In the regular forces there is a considerable

amount of encouragement given to the married women in order to have their husbands remain in the services.
There is quite a bit of attention paid to the attitude of the women in this connection until the husband is killed in what those of us who have served and others think is the course of his duty; then the Department of National Defence and the Department of Veterans Affairs say, "There is nothing we can do about it under section 13(2). This accident did not arise out of service". They say to the widow, "Although for several years your husband served his country gallantly in war and in peace, we are sorry but we cannot do anything for you now. You may have children. Well, that is not our responsibility, and you must go somewhere else."
I do not think we can much longer tolerate that state of affairs under legislation which is so frequently described here as the best veterans' charter in the world, and so on. If things of this nature continue to be permitted it must certainly be revised if it is to become the best in the world.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I could not give the hon. member at this time the exact number of applications that were turned down on that specific basis. The question of pre-enlistment condition is
Supply-Veterans Affairs dealt with in section 13, subsection 1 (c) of the act. The principle is that no deduction is ever made in the award because of a preenlistment condition where there has been service in a theatre of war, unless prior to enlistment the condition was obvious or recorded on medical examination.
The meaning of the words "recorded on medical examination" appears in section 2, subsection (u) of the Pension Act. That is a definition that was inserted in 1948 at the suggestion of the members of the veterans affairs committee. In order to understand this section properly, one should read the definition of the words "recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment". Subsection (u) reads as follows:
(u)	"recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment'' includes recorded symptoms or findings in,
(i)	medical proceedings for enlistment,
(ii)	official documentation covering any former period of service,
(iii)	the files of the department,
(iv)	compensation board or insurance company records, and
(v)	the records of a hospital, private physician or other medical authority,
where such record refers to the injury or disease resulting in the disability in respect of which the application for pension is made;
As my hon. friend says, this covers considerable ground. It is quite true that some members of the forces-I understand that this occurred more often during the first war than during the second war-were accepted as being in good physical condition and after being discharged from the service developed certain conditions for which a claim for pension was made. When the commission goes back into the army records, it might be found that a man had been hospitalized in 1942 or 1943 for a certain condition. Then going back into hospital records, they might find that, on being questioned as to his medical history upon entering hospital, he had said that when 10 or 15 years of age he had been hospitalized for a certain condition. The commission might get in touch with the doctor who had looked after him at that particular time. The man might not be familiar with what had happened, but when the doctor was contacted it might be discovered that the condition for which the man was claiming was pre-enlistment. This information would not be withheld wilfully by the man when enlisting, as he might not be aware of this condition, but the commission would find that as part of his medical record, and under the statute it could do nothing but take it into consideration.
