Further to what the hon. member for Macleod has said, I should like to pursue this matter a little. I have in my hands the particulars of a case where a man claims that upon enlistment he was found to be in category A. After enlistment he was re-examined four times and always found to be in category A. The man enlisted on May 19, 1941, and left the service on June 3, 1942. He was discharged at that time for medical reasons but was denied full pension benefits because it was claimed that the medical reasons for his discharge had existed prior to enlistment.
I find this a little hard to swallow. We are willing to send a man over the hill, as it were, upon the basis of one medical examination, provided he is declared to be in category A. If we are willing to risk a man's life on the basis of one physical examination he should receive the proper consideration. Former students of mine lost their lives after having had only one medical examination, yet here is a case where a man was declared five times to be in category A.
I notice that in replying to the hon. member for Macleod the minister qualified his statement by saying that a pension decision was partly dependent upon where the service had been. I think that is a most despicable arrangement if such an arrangement exists. Once a man volunteers his life on behalf of the nation he should receive equal treatment regardless of the disposition that is made of that man by the armed forces.


I should like to read from the report of the pensions advocate concerning this man, as follows:
Service documents record treatment for the above noted condition during service. During treatment he stated he had had many colds in his head and pleurisy at eight or nine years of age.
May I just interrupt here. I wonder if this man had asked for exemption from military service on the basis of having had this condition when eight or nine years of age how far he would have got. He would not have got to first base, especially after having five medical examinations which listed him as being in category A. I continue:
According to specialist's report, on 14-4-42, man gave a history that he saw Dr. Campbell Brown in Vernon, B.C., because of frequent colds in chest with cough. On the record this condition existed pre-enlistment with some aggravation during service, but there is no evidence to show that such aggravation arose out of or was directly connected with military service.
I must interrupt to say again that this man was found to be in category A in five examinations. I continue with the report:
The commission rules chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis pre-enlistment condition, aggravated during service in Canada but not pensionable under section 11 (2) as the aggravation did not arise out of nor was it directly connected with military service.
I feel the minister must agree that this is a most niggardly attitude to take when we are willing to shove men over the hill upon the basis of one report which lists them in category A; yet when after five listings in A category these men are thrown out of the service, even against their will, and declared medically unfit and they apply for a pension, we say, "We have now discovered, because of the statement the man made in all honesty at the time of his enlistment, that he had a cold when he was a child, and we therefore find that the disability is of pre-enlistment origin." I think that is disgraceful.

I feel I must rise to join with others who are discussing the situation of veterans who, after entering military service and getting a clean bill of health, then have disabilities and find, perhaps after demobilization or discharge, that they are not eligible for pension. It is not my intention at this time to go fully into the case I have had before the department for some three years, but I feel that since other hon. members have spoken on this very issue, I too must make mention of it.
In the case of the veteran of whom I am speaking, he was examined by six specialists of the department on enlistment. He was a first war veteran, having served some three and a half years, and he enlisted for second war service. His category on enlistment for

second war service was Al; he came out P5. He was not demobilized but discharged with the lowest possible category. As I understand it, the terms of the veterans' act are that a veteran is entitled on discharge to be boarded for a medical examination. This man was not boarded for a medical examination, and the determination of his disabilities was not made until 1949. When they were found it was established that he had a heart condition. I have a letter, which is before the department, confirming that he at least feels that his disability was due to service, and the symptoms were those he was boarded for health reasons during his service.
In spite of the fact that many of us bring veterans' cases before the department in which we obtain good consideration and fair and just settlements, it seems to me that in this particular case, where a veteran has served with distinction and has come out with such a low category and there is an establishment of a severe disability, it is up to the pension commission to grant such a veteran some reasonable pension. I want to say to the minister that I intend to fight this case until I get some pension for him that will be in conformity with his service and his disability.
I do not think we can be satisfied with a situation in which a man, having served his country for 10J- years, should be treated in such a way. He was not demobilized but was discharged. As a matter of fact this particular veteran was kept on the staff here in Ottawa for six months after demobilization because the department could not do without his services. To turn him out and to leave the onus of proof on him is completely incompatible with the act, I think, and certainly with simple justice. So I just want to inform the minister that I hope in the near future there will be an easement on the part of the pension commission so the veterans in these cases coming before them will not have the onus of proof put on their shoulders when they cannot establish the exact date when their disabilities occurred. If the veteran has five or six medicals on enlistment, comes out in a P5 category, and is discharged on that account, surely he should be entitled to a decent pension.
So I hope we members of the opposition will not have to get up again and plead with the minister of this department for an easement and an adjustment on behalf of these servicemen. I hope we shall have some justice and that they will receive pensions when they come out with such a low category.

I am very pleased indeed to hear from the minister that the veterans are the most reliable credit customers we have in Canada. I think he would agree that in relation to the vast number concerned, almost all of them are meeting their commitments on the due dates. I believe he mentioned some 40 or so out of 31,000 who were in arrears. I think that is something really worthy of note in Canada and even in Canadian credit circles.
I also noticed that in reply to the hon. member for Acadia he mentioned that even today there were some veterans of the first world war who were owing money on their properties. I think 99-9 per cent of the people of Canada would be most happy to see the minister this year, not next year, introduce a bill into this House of Commons that would wipe out this balance owing by these senior citizens and senior veterans of our country. However, my main reason for rising at this time is to ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to raising the amount of the loan that it is permissible to be granted to the veterans of the recent world war on the purchase of small holdings.
In my riding the cost of small holdings consists mainly of the cost of the home. Whereas several years ago $8,400 may have supplied the veteran with an adequate home, that is not the situation today. I might at this time pay my compliments to the civil servants in this branch of the minister's department. I think many of the finest homes were built by veterans at that time for that money. However, has any consideration been given to the greatly increased cost of the land and also of the buildings since that time? I hate to see these two by four buildings going up. For $8,400 nowadays in my riding you cannot put up a home that is worthy of erection, one that will be a credit to Canada and that will be in line with what the veteran deserves. It costs us at least $10 a square foot to put up even the most modest of homes. I feel that we have had enough of these small homes built in Canada. Most of these veterans' families have now reached an age where they need larger homes.
I am wondering whether any consideration has been given, during the last year or so,

If a veteran wants to take advantage of the veterans' legislation I see no reason why he should be obliged to build an $8,000 home when other Canadian citizens, taking advantage of the provisions of the National Housing Act guaranteed loans, can move into $13,000, $14,000 and $15,000 homes. speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources includes five branches that deal with widely divergent subjects. The national parks branch administers the national parks of Canada, the national historic parks and historic sites, the Canadian wildlife service and the national museum. The water resources branch is responsible for the federal aspects of water resource questions in Canada. The northern administration and lands branch handles the administration of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory in all its aspects. It is responsible for the administration of Eskimo affairs and also for a great many land problems including the natural resources of the two territories. The forestry branch deals with forest research, forest products research, and forestry management, including agreements with the provinces on forest inventories and reforestation. The Canadian government travel bureau deals with travel promotion and the tourist industry in so far as they are of concern to the federal government.
With this great variety of operations I do not think it would be desirable for me to try to give a comprehensive survey of the work of the department in detail at this time. Such a survey was given when the estimates of my department were before the committee on estimates during last session, and many hon. members will be familiar with the discussion at that time. In all the circumstances I think it may be more satisfactory to deal with a few of the highlights of departmental operations as reflected in the estimates for the coming year. I would wish also to outline in some detail the policy of the department with regard to national parks. When each individual branch is under consideration I shall, of course, be very happy to deal in detail with particular aspects of the work in which any hon. members might be interested.
A principal point of interest in the estimates of any department is always the extent of and the reasons for any major changes from the preceding year. For 1956-57 the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources show an increase of $5,918,662 in the main estimates, plus an additional $3,084,078 in the supplementary

estimates. This makes a total increase of $9,002,740. The increase, as a percentage of the estimates for 1955-56 is quite substantial, approximately 30 per cent. It is my hope that the house will feel that this increase is entirely justified, in fact I would venture to say more than justified, because of the reasons that lie behind the increases where they occur. The actual increases are in fact concentrated in a very few major aspects of operation, and these aspects reflect the places in which the government feels that substantial increases in activity are necessary.
The largest single increase is in the appropriation for the construction of trunk highways and bridges in the national parks. This increase amounts to $4,687,450, including the main and supplementary estimates. There are over 500 miles of main highways in the various national parks. This does not include those portions of the trans-Canada highway that are in the parks, nor does it include minor roads and trails.
These main highways include such important roads as the Banff-Jasper highway; the Banff-Windermere highway; the highways north and south through Prince Albert national park and Riding Mountain national park; the highway connecting with the provincial highways in Fundy national park; the Cabot trail in Cape Breton Highlands national park; and the Ocean View highway in Prince Edward Island national park.
The traffic on these roads has been increasing very markedly in the last few years. The extent and rate of the increase in traffic has now gone far beyond the standards to which most of these highways were built. In virtually all cases extensive or complete reconstruction is becoming necessary. I might also mention that we have found, particularly in the mountain parks, that it is very poor economy to build roads that are below the standard that is required for the wear and tear that the traffic imposes on them. The government, accordingly, has approved a six-year program for the reconstruction of the major park roads.
The total program over the six years will, it is presently estimated, amount to over $60 million. The increase in 1956-57 represents the first instalment of this new program. It includes major construction activity on the Banff-Windermere highway; the Banff-Jasper highway, the Cabot trail, and the Ocean View highway. The program in succeeding years will, on the average, be somewhat greater than the level indicated in this year's estimates.
Other capital items in the parks constitute an increase of $849,118. Accordingly, of
67509-376i
Supply-Northern Affairs the total departmental increase I have mentioned, no less than $5,529,568 is made up by construction and other capital items in the national parks.
The next largest item of increase also reflects an expansion of activity as a result of decisions of policy. This increase is in capital items in the north. One of the major requirements in the Northwest Territories is to provide the kind of educational facilities that will equip the Indian and Eskimo children there for the change that is now taking place at an increasingly rapid rate from their native hunting and trapping economy to an economy based on our way of life. This is not a change, at least in the rate it is taking place, that has been particularly sought or worked for at this time. I dealt in more detail with this matter in the statement on education policy that I made before the committee on estimates last year and I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to go into it at length now.
I might say, however, that the present change is a change that is inevitable because of two interrelated forces. One is the very great increase in economic, defence and other activity in the north that is bringing our way of life inevitably into contact with the native way of life. The other is the fact that the hunting and trapping economy is rapidly becoming less capable of supporting the increasing population. Unless a very serious human problem is to be faced in a few years, extensive education and training of the native people to face a new form of life is urgently required. The largest single increase in northern administration is to provide educational facilities, housing and related administrative facilities in the Northwest Territories. It amounts to $1,821,565, of which educational facilities alone form by far the largest part.
The other substantial aspect of increase in northern administration reflects the policy of the government to stimulate and encourage economic development in the north. The increase for the construction of roads and bridges amounts to $441,830. The increase in funds provided for the construction of the new Aklavik as a centre for administration, education, and welfare in the far north amounts to $1,013,650. These three capital figures are subject to an adjustment downward of $1 million, which was the original estimate of likely short-fall in northern operations, and which has been partly restored in the supplementary estimates. The net result is that the increase of a capital character in our northern administration amounts in total, including the main and supplementary estimates, to $2,277,045.
As hon. members will see from what I have said, the total departmental increase is made
5928	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs up to the extent of $7,806,613 by capital items in the national parks and the two northern territories.
The other substantial increase in the departmental appropriations again reflects a capital item. For a number of years the government has been providing an annual grant to the pulp and paper research institute to assist in the financing of research that is of value to this very important part of the Canadian forest industry. As was announced some months ago, it has now been agreed with the institute that it would be preferable for the government to provide a building of the most modern and efficient character in which research can be carried on and to discontinue the annual grants. There is, therefore, in the estimates an amount of $1,075,000 for a new laboratory to be constructed in Montreal. The total costs of the lab with equipment, to be financed by the federal government, will amount to $2,250,000 over a two-year period.
I think the above summary sets forth virtually all the substantial increases in the appropriations that are now being sought. The capital figures I have mentioned account for increases of $8,881,613. There are minor increases and some decreases in other places which bring the total departmental increase to the figure I gave at the beginning of my remarks, $9,002,740.
There is one other highlight of departmental activity that I should like to mention. As hon. members are aware, water problems have for some time been of concern in the province of Manitoba. As a result of discussions with Premier Campbell, I signed an agreement with him on July 5 for the establishment of a lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba

board. The board will consist of representatives of the province and of the federal government, and its duties will be to-and I quote from the agreement-
. . . plan, supervise and carry out a study of lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba and the resources of water within Manitoba flowing into and from those lakes.
It is to report on:
. . . what further developments and controls of these water resources in its judgment would appear to be physically practicable with particular reference to (a) flood control; and (b) hydroelectric power.
The federal government and the province are sharing equally in the cost of the survey and report.
Mr. Chairman, as I said at the beginning of my remarks I had intended to go on for some time in outlining the policy of the department regarding national parks, but since it is two minutes before ten o'clock I might call it ten o'clock at this time.

Mr. Chairman,
I listened with a great deal of interest yesterday to the many members who took part in the discussion of the estimates of this department. There is no doubt that all members are interested in the problems of the veterans. It is not my intention to review all that was said yesterday, but there are a few comments that I wish to bring to the minister's attention, and I hope that they will be useful and that good will come out of them.
There is in my constituency one of the finest, if not the finest, veterans' hospitals in Canada. I have watched its growth from the very day when the property was acquired and the original buildings were built at the close of the first world war up until this day. I am acquainted with many of the doctors and members of the staff of the hospital, and I want to pay a word of tribute and praise to the work of the doctors, the nurses and the staff at the hospital. It is understandable that, where there are such a large number of patients in a hospital covering such a wide area, there naturally will be some complaints and perhaps some injustices, but in most cases these complaints are taken care of in a very efficient way, and I think most of the people are well satisfied with the services they are given.
While I am mentioning Westminster hospital I might say that in 1953 I also referred to the old buildings that were erected there at the close of the first world war, and the minister at that time indicated that some new buildings were proposed. Some additions have been made, and I hope the minister will indicate to the house that the rest of the old buildings will very shortly be removed and new buildings erected in their place. I should be glad if he would later indicate such to the house. I should just say, too, that I am glad that the minister and his department have taken into consideration those pensions between 40 per cent and 45 per cent. I think that action will meet with general approval. I think it is advisable to establish a plan or system of periodic reviews of all pensions and pension cases because the conditions of health change from time to time, as we all know. But there are many pensioners who hesitate to ask for a review of their particular case and there are others who do not hesitate. Sometimes there are many worthy cases that do not get the attention to which they are probably entitled.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
I speak for those pensioners who sometimes are denied a pension because their particular illness or complaint is alleged to have been attributable to causes arising before they enlisted or to post-discharge causes. I have in mind one or two of those particular cases in which it is alleged that the disability is so attributable. Yet these men served in the armed forces for several years. They were passed as being A-l, were accepted and were able to discharge their duties overseas. Yet, when they come back it is said that their disability arises because there was some illness prior to their enlistment.
There is no doubt-and this is well known to the department and to everyone here- that the earning capacity of many veterans has been reduced because of war service in one way or another. Some of them were not able to complete their education. Through disabilities some could not carry on their intended life work. The increase in the rate of pension that was granted a short time ago is still inadequate, in my opinion, in view of the inflation and the present cost of living. Also, the ceilings of earnings are too low considering living costs and the pension level.
I would just say that the grant that was given a short time ago certainly could not be considered to be extravagant. I do not think it would even be considered to be liberal.
Back in 1951 and prior to that time I mentioned in this house the suggestion that the pensions-not only those for war service but also old age pensions-should be hooked to the cost of living index. I am still of that opinion. If that were done, if you once establish what is a fair and right pension level, then as the cost of living goes up the pension would go up; and if sometime in the future the cost of living goes down, the pension could also go down. In that way the income from the pension would bear some relation to its purchasing power and there would not always be these questions arising: it being said that the pension is not high enough and that the cost of living has gone up, and then, after two or three years have elapsed, an amendment being introduced with a view to increasing the pension. This suggestion would eliminate all this problem. Also I had in my constituency four V.L.A. small holding areas, one in London township and two or three in Westminster. I am very well acquainted with the officials there, and at this point I should say that I believe they are doing a very fine job. There are very few complaints. While I am doing that, I should also pay tribute to the young veterans who have taken up these holdings. They

Supply-Veterans Affairs have taken great pride in their homes, improved their properties and they are not only taking an interest but taking part in the community in which they live, in the public life of the community through municipal affairs and church affairs. I might say that it was my privilege to have as a guest in Middlesex East the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, who addressed the veterans there some time ago. I believe that he also was greatly impressed with the community spirit and the work that they are doing.
Now, I come to the question I asked on Monday regarding the five-day 40-hour week for Westminster hospital employees and the employees of veterans hospitals in other parts of the country, who are asking that they be given the same hours of work as the employees of other departmental hospitals. I listened to the minister's explanation, and then I read the translation of his answer to the hon. member for Quebec West. While the minister has not denied to these employees the five-day 40-hour week, I think that regardless of what employment conditions may be in other industries or in other hospitals in any particular city, all the employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs should be treated similarly, whether they be in London, Halifax, Calgary or any other place. I believe it has been amply demonstrated that the employees of these hospitals can give efficient and continuous service, day and night, on the five-day 40-hour week. Consequently I am asking the minister to seriously consider the representations that have been made to him here and by the employees association last October. I ask him not to let this session go by without granting equality to all employees of the veterans hospitals across Canada.

I regret, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not seen fit at this session to introduce any legislation to improve the position of the recipients of war veterans allowance. The hon. member for Royal and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra went into this matter in considerable detail, so I am not going to take the time of the house to give reasons why action along that line should be taken. However, I would say I have never been able to understand why the government was not willing at least to raise the amount of the permissive income. For many years past I have urged, as have others, that the limit on the permissive income should be increased to at least the amount of the income tax exemptions. I would urge the government to bring in legislation at the next session to put that into effect, as well as 
to increase the actual amounts paid to recipients of war veterans allowances.
There is another matter on which perhaps I can get some information from the minister when we come to the details, but I should like to mention it at this time. I refer to the amounts paid by veterans who are not receiving disability pensions for medical attention and hospitalization. A resolution was passed by Calgary branch No. 1, my own branch of the Canadian Legion, in regard to this matter which reads as follows:
Free medical treatment for all veterans over 55 years of age with meritorious service with annual incomes in the case of single men of less than $1,800 and in the case of married men of less than $3,500.
The amount charged veterans who are not entitled to hospitalization has been increased I believe twice in the last few years, and is now in the neighbourhood of $14 per day. A married man with an income of less than $3,500 or a single man with an income of less than $1,800 finds it most difficult to pay that amount, especially when they are over 55 years of age. I should mention that they would not have to pay the full $14 per day as the amount is reduced according to income received. I submit that veterans in those income tax brackets should be given the benefits of hospitalization without payment. I should like the minister to say something about this matter of hospitalization and take under advisement the question of liberalizing the hospitalization policy in order to protect older veterans on comparatively small incomes.
I should like next to say something about the work of the imperial war graves commission. I had the opportunity last summer of seeing Canadian war cemeteries in northwestern Europe and Italy where Canadians who fought in both world wars are buried. I think I can say that without doubt they constitute the finest group of cemeteries to be found anywhere in the world. The care which they are given and the architecture which has been used to fit them into their backgrounds are of an extremely high order. I wish that every person who has a relative buried in one of those cemeteries had the opportunity to go to see it. I am glad that a grant is given to the imperial war graves commission under this department and I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to commend them upon the work they have done in maintaining the graves of our men who are buried overseas.
There is one other matter I should like to take up at this time, the question of compensation to members of the non-permanent militia, and to some extent the members of the permanent forces, when accidents occur which disable them or which result in death.

I bring this up particularly because of a case which occurred in Calgary last year. In outlining this case and referring to some of the difficulties that exist with regard to the legislation I want to make it quite clear that I am in no way reflecting upon the members of the pension commission. The chairman of the pension commission has done an outstanding job and I think he and the other members have carried on their activities with a very high sense of duty. The difficulty concerning cases of this sort, I think, primarily lies in the way the legislation reads and I think an amendment to the legislation in this regard is long overdue. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre mentioned the matter briefly yesterday and referred to the section of the act which deals with pensions to people who come under this classification. He indicated there had been considerable discussion of the matter when the estimates of this department were before the estimates committee last year but that no action had been taken concerning it. I would hope that some definite action would be taken in the near future.
The particular case I wish to give as an illustration of what happens concerns a squadron sergeant major in the South Alberta Light Horse. This man had a good record; he served overseas for five years and was awarded the military medal and he served six years in the militia. The unit is quite widely spread with one detachment at Strathmore some 40 miles from Calgary. They were in Calgary having an Armistice day celebration parade and so forth. The commanding officer of the unit got permission from western command headquarters in Edmonton to send a detachment down to take part in this anniversary day service and parade. Apparently the military transport in the form of a bus or busses had not arrived when the men gathered at the armoury in Calgary. They received a message to the effect that the bus had broken down or had been delayed in some way. The 2/IC of the regiment who was present told the men to take their own private cars. There happened to be a sufficient number of the men who had private cars to provide transportation for all of them, the presumption being that these men would eventually be reimbursed for their gasoline and expenses. In any event they proceeded to Strathmore and on the way back this particular sergeant major and another man were killed in the automobile which was driven by the other man. There was apparently no question of guilt or negligence so far as the driver was concerned and the widow of the
Supply-Veterans Affairs sergeant major was not able to take action against the driver or his estate as the result of the death of her husband.
She applied for the pension and her application was turned down at the first hearing. The decision of the commission was as follows:
Death incurred during military service in peacetime, but not pensionable under section 13 (2) as on the evidence presently available there is nothing to indicate death arose out of or was directly connected with such service.
A second hearing was held in this case and again her application was denied. I do not know whether it will be appealed but I presume it will be. The decision arises because section 13 (2) as it reads and has been interpreted makes it obligatory on the part of the person requesting the pension to prove in a case of this sort that the man was riding in a military vehicle, as I understand it, or a vehicle which had definitely been taken on strength for the time being and for which the man was being paid a mileage allowance.
In this particular case the man was on military duty and it happened through circumstances beyond his control that the military transportation did not turn up. The men were authorized by the senior officer there to use their private cars and it was in those circumstances that this man was killed. His widow's pension was denied but she would have received it if he had been killed in the military bus. It seems to me the interpretation of the act is much too narrow. The act is drawn in such a way as to cause an injustice of this sort.
I would ask the minister and the pensions commission to take this particular case under consideration again. It seems to me it might be possible by ministerial direction or by order in council that something could be done without its being necessary to change the act. I realize there probably is not time during this session to change the act but I think it would be possible by the means I have indicated to give direction to the commission to interpret this particular clause more liberally than is the case now; in other words, to interpret it in the spirit it was conceived to have when it was passed by this House of Commons. I am certain there was never any intention on the part of parliament that the widow of a man who was killed on military duty should be denied a pension because of an accident of the type I have mentioned where a military vehicle was not supplied although it was supposed to have been supplied and a private vehicle was authorized instead.
The same sort of thing applies to some extent to permanent force personnel. I was

Supply-Veterans Affairs interested in a case which had an unfavourable first and second hearing and I believe was eventually settled satisfactorily on appeal. This case involved a man who was killed overseas. Only with great difficulty was it established that he was on military duty and his widow was able to get a pension. This occurred some two or three years ago. Eventually she was able to establish the fact and was granted a pension. The circumstances were much the same as in the previous case I mentioned except that in this instance a military jeep was used. There was some difficulty in establishing that the trip it was on had been properly authorized and that the man was properly on duty, as I recall the circumstances. In any event, however, it was finally settled satisfactorily.
It seems to me that in the cases I have mentioned a little more attention should be paid to the spirit of the legislation. If this were done I believe the first case could be settled in a way that would be satisfactory to the widow and other dependents of this soldier. I certainly hope the minister will give some personal attention to this matter and will see what can be done without its being necessary to change the legislation; as I indicated before, it is perhaps too late in the session for that to be done.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to compliment the minister on the keen interest he has shown in the affairs of veterans especially during the last two or three years. I wish to thank him personally for the courtesy he has always shown me when I have brought personal cases to his attention-and this applies also to his staff in general.
I suppose I should compliment the staff because they carry out the letter of the law, but at the same time I also complain that the letter of the law is predominant in the administration of the veterans legislation and I think the spirit of the law and not the legal interpretation should prevail. It is on that subject that I wish to say a few words at this time.
In order to overcome the difficulty I have mentioned it seems to me a little more leeway should be given to the local administrators, those people who know the local problems and the persons involved. They are far more conversant with the individual cases and are better equipped to find solutions to the various problems than is someone in Ottawa or possibly in Vancouver or Calgary. I think that if a little more power were given to them to interpret the law according to the spirit of the act, many of the problems about which we are now worrying would be solved.
[Mr. Harkness.l

In many instances cases which are recommended to be dealt with in a certain way by local officials who know the circumstances have been turned down by senior administrators who have given a narrow interpretation to the wording of the act. The justice of the case did not enter into it, the morality of the case did not enter into it, the spirit of the case did not enter into it; there was simply a pure, logical reasoning as to the legality of the act.
I was a member of the veterans committee when it sat and I know the attention that was given to any question that came up. I know the feeling of all hon. members that the veteran should be given the benefit of any doubt, yet in practice this is not always done. I could outline the details quite quickly, but I shall not do so at this time. This is my main reason for advocating the setting up of a permanent veterans committee. I think it would be a far more important committee than many of those that now go on year after year, sometimes going through a session without meeting. Such a committee would carry out most important functions of great value to the minister and to the veterans.
Without such a committee we are in danger of gradually building up a legal bureaucracy, a group without a heart, a legal entity ready to carry out only, the letter of the law. If we had a veterans committee dealing with cases, that atmosphere would be changed when a veteran had to appear before a board or other group. I am sure that neither parliament nor the people of Canada wish this condition to continue.
It is true that we have made progress equal to that made in any other country, but there are many problems still unsolved affecting the veteran. I would mention those veterans who served in England during the first world war. Their number is getting smaller each year but they are still denied the right of pension. The hon. member for Kootenay West referred yesterday to two men who had joined up and who served as clerks, one in England and one in France. The one man is receiving a pension while the other is denied a pension. Such discrepancies should be removed and all veterans treated on a fair basis.
I still think that we should make the permissive income under the War Veterans Allowance Act more in keeping with the cost of living today, and the widows of veterans who have resided in Canada for some years should be recognized as being pensionable. I shall not go into the details of these cases, as the minister knows them better than I do.

Another problem which could be dealt with by a committee sitting year after year is one such as has cropped up recently in British Columbia, and this may be true also of other parts of Canada. British Columbia has recently made a reassessment of properties for school tax purposes. I have here a resolution which I should like to place on the record so the minister may know what I am talking about. It reads:
Whereas the reassessment of property in British Columbia which has recently taken place, grave concern is felt for veterans occupying small holdings under the Veterans Land Act, having their holdings of one acre, reclassified from agricultural into residential districts resulting in an increased assessment of at least double the original amount and a good chance of increased taxes due to present tendency of real estate speculation, which surround the V.L.A. project. This particularly' applies to about 60 veterans located in the BankHead district near Kelowna, B.C. These veterans were rehabilitated on these acre lots with a view of their being able to supplement their earnings, now the reassessment will defeat the government's original intention and following the pattern of the first world war veteran, will force the veteran to vacate his holding as was the case of very many of our older veterans, who had taken up land under the Soldier Settlement Land Act and who were forced to quit, because of economic conditions.
Therefore, be it resolved that this north Okanagan zone request the provincial command to make strong representations to the provincial government protesting the reassessment of V.L.A. small holdings into residential areas and thus enable them to derive the benefit which has been granted to them under the veterans charter.
I appreciate that this is probably a provincial problem, but nevertheless the Department of Veterans Affairs has a responsibility to look after the interests of these veterans. In my opinion the least they can do is to protest to the provincial or municipal authorities this reassessment-in this case it is the province-on the ground that the veteran is entitled to special benefits. These men went on these small holdings with the understanding that benefits would accrue to them as long as they occupied the land.
The hon. member for Calgary North referred to the problem of the man who is killed while technically not on duty. Whether or not a man is on duty, I submit he is still a soldier. One or two cases have occurred recently in my riding. A young fellow who had served three years in Germany took a ride in a civilian car and was killed. This case is similar to the one mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North. This man leaves a widow and two children and so far they have not received a cent from any department of government. They cannot qualify under this act; they cannot qualify under the army or in any other way that I can find out.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
It seems to me that any man who joins the forces should be granted protection at all times for accident and death in order that the widow and orphans he may leave behind shall be protected. In this case the widow and the two orphans are living on charity. It seems to me that every soldier on joining the forces should be given the protection of an insurance policy to cover everything that may happen, with provision for the payment of at least $20,000 to his widow and family in the event of his death. There is a moral obligation to protect these young men in every way. They are depending entirely upon the army for their income and the welfare of their families should be protected.
We have not met this particular problem. I do not blame the department for this, but I hope the department will co-operate with the Department of National Defence in an effort to find a solution something like that mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North so that in future we will not be faced with cases of this kind.
Another problem concerns the farmer settler. I am not going to go into detail about this matter because I have already written to the minister and he has kindly promised to look into it. Last year several farmers in the Cawston area of British Columbia suffered severe frost damage to their young orchards. They lost most of their trees which had to be replaced or replanted and they will have to wait for five or six years before they get a crop. It seems to me that the local V. L. A. authorities should be given full power to go into that area to assess the damage and what it would cost the Department of Veterans Affairs to replace these trees in order that these young farmers may be rehabilitated. If that is not done, I am afraid many of them will abandon their farms. They have been there two or three years struggling along and waiting for the time when they would have a crop. That time has now been deferred for another four, five or six years. I hope the minister will pay special attention to this group.
Another problem arises from legal interpretation. This concerns a case of young men who have gone out to work while their farms were coming into production. The case I have in mind is typical of two or three other cases that I know of. This young man was told on his return from service that he had to go on a farm for at least two years to qualify as a full-time farmer. He did so and qualified. He returned to the board, and they accepted his qualifications. On the strength of that, he went and purchased 35 acres of land; I presume it was part fruit and part stock, but whether it is fruit or stock the

Supply-Veterans Affairs same applies: he would have no income for at least three years. With that in mind he thought he would get help and that he would work in his spare time, taking a job outside. As soon as he said he was going to work outside for three years until the farm would support him, he was refused the ordinary assistance under the act. The interpretation in this case, I claim, again was too narrow. True, the board in Vancouver is going to re-hear the case. In this case the local office, who know the man, who know the land and who know the conditions fully approved but somewhere-I call them "armchair farmers" -some administrators decided on the case. No armchair farmer can tell as much as local people what a young man is capable of doing or what the land is capable of producing.
Finally, I would suggest to the minister that the time has now arrived when those veterans of the first world war who are still struggling with the remains of a mortgage should have that mortgage cleared and a clear title given to them. It would not cost too much. I know the policy of taking care of them year after year has been carried out, but many of these people are now getting to an age where it is worrying them. They are too old to stand the strain, and that strain should be removed by giving a clear title to a veteran who has been on his land for 20, 30 or as in some cases, 40 years.

I should just like to say a word or two on this item and in doing so I think I shall have to follow what others have said in respect to my belief that the veterans' legislation that we have on the statute books of Canada ranks perhaps with some of the best veterans legislation of any country in the world. That has been said before, and I think it will stand repeating. I think we have all had a part in bringing about that legislation. Suggestions have been made in previous veterans affairs committees, and with an efficient staff and an interest in the returned man I think we have accomplished something along that line.
I wish also now to pay my respects to the minister and thank him for very courteously taking up any cases I have presented to him. I recognize that he is confined within the regulations and within the law, but I am happy with the attitude he takes when I present cases to him, passing them on to his officials, doing some little personal investigation and trying to solve those particular cases, if possible.
I have handled a good many veterans' cases over the years, and on the whole there seems to be one general type of case which I do not think is quite fairly treated. This


matter has been mentioned before over and over again, I fancy, and perhaps the veterans affairs committees have wrestled with this problem. That is the problem of the returned man's health at the time of enlistment, when he is given the category of an A1 condition and then, after he applies for a pension because in his mind and perhaps in the minds of many others he has a good case for a pension, somehow or other in the investigation by doctors and other interested officials they go back to a predetermined period and say, "This originates by reason of something that happened before you enlisted."
I think I can say that in most of the cases I have had to take up with the minister in respect to war veterans' pensions that seems to have been the main problem. I cannot let the estimates go by without adding my voice to the voices of others in making this strong plea that, if a veteran is taken into the defence forces and given an A1 category as his condition at the time, then that should remain the category of the veteran, unless of course the veteran at the time of recruitment purposely falsified the record or perhaps evaded certain questions or refused to give the full information. Unless this can be proved, then I think that the condition at enlistment should be regarded as his actual physical condition. If through his war services something happens to him, then I think he is reasonable enough in asking for a pension and should be given it regardless of pre-enlistment condition.
This is not a new thing. The minister knows all about it, and I wish he would make some pronouncement as to why this is so. I have never been able to satisfy myself that a reasonable explanation has ever been given as to why they should search into preenlistment causes when at the time of enlistment the man was given a clean bill of health. The recruiting officials seem to take the attitude, "We will try to put the man in the army if we can possibly get him through." That may not be so but that is how it seems to me. If he is thoroughly examined according to the regulations of recruitment, then I claim that that examination should be sufficient, unless it is found later, as I said before, that the recruit is purposely falsifying the record or purposely withholding some information. I wish the minister would once again give his pronouncement on that.
There is one other matter: a permanent veterans affairs committee. That has been mentioned before, and I do not wish to take up the time of the house on it now. I am sure our group would agree to having this committee made a permanent committee, and if it is not recognized as a standing committee

it should be set up every year anyway. I cannot see any reason why it should not be because it is not going to cost much money. The committee is run by the House of Commons. Those members who sit on the committee are not paid any extra stipend for that work. Of course a clerk is required and some printing is required, but apart from that it does not cost very much. The small expense is absorbed in the general appropriation that we give for the work of the House of Commons. I think the minister could also comment on that and say just why he thinks it is not reasonable to set up a veterans affairs committee every year.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to repeat any of the arguments that have been advanced but there are one or two matters that I think I should bring to the attention of the committee, especially as no hon. member from Saskatchewan has spoken since these estimates have been before the committee. So far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, the records show that 66,614 Saskatchewan residents wore a uniform in either or both wars, 16,002 in world war I, 48,263 in world war II and 2,349 in both wars. I also do so because over the years, too many years for one to be willing to admit, I have been a member of the Canadian Legion in Prince Albert and I wish to place before the minister and the committee some of the ideas and suggestions that Saskatchewan branch No. 2 and other branches have brought to my attention.
I want to say at once that so far as the pension commission is concerned my experience has been that Brigadier Melville and those associated with him have given to each individual case that has come within my knowledge and cognizance the very fullest of considerate attention. That is as it should be, for after all the commission should not permit itself to be shackled by a too close interpretation of the letter of the law and by a denial in consequence of the spirit of the law. The only criticisms that one hears from time to time arise out of individual cases. I can think of no better description of the pension commission than the words used by a cadet sergeant named Dwight Eisenhower who contributed an article in 1915 to his West Point class paper which began in this way: "True merit is like a river. The deeper it is the less noise it makes." This organization has not made any noise over the contribution that it has made, but that does not mean that individual cases have not arisen that deserve the serious reconsideration of the board of pension commissioners. Mention was made by the member for Calgary North of the Stanley Hepworth case. I am going to refer to it for a moment because in my 67509-3744
Supply-Veterans Affairs opinion the widow is legally entitled to a pension on behalf of herself and her children. The decision of the commission, as recorded in a letter I have before me, is as follows:

My only regret is that the government is unwilling to grant in their entirety

the requests of the Canadian Legion. After all, these men were willing to sacrifice all in defence of democracy.
The Liberal party was not willing to sacrifice all in defence of democracy. I well remember that when the last war was at its height the C.C.F. party was advocating that we risk all in defence of democracy including not only the lives of these men but also the possessions of the people of Canada. However, the Liberal party saw fit at that time to risk only the lives of Canadian citizens. The time has come for us to pay tribute to those who risked all at that time.
I see that we are prepared to spend 5 per cent of the income of this government in order to help those who were willing to risk all. We are prepared to spend 40 per cent of our income on possible future wars. The Department of National Defence is asking for 40 cents out of our dollar whereas the Department of Veterans Affairs is asking for only 5 cents out of our dollar. I feel the balance is rather out of line, Mr. Chairman. I feel that if we want the Canadian people to be sincere in their effort in any future war-and I hope it will not occur- the relationship of the 5 per cent and 40 per cent will have to be brought into line. I can understand some of the hesitancy on the part of the government to grant a larger measure of welfare to our veterans when I think of the attitude of the government to the cause of democracy. These people-most of them at least-were willing to sacrifice their lives for our way of life and for our system of government which is exemplified by the parliament of Canada, and yet the Liberal party has been able to accomplish what Kaiser Wilhelm and Adolf Hitler were unable to accomplish. The Kaiser of Germany went all out to destroy democracy and Adolf Hitler made a supreme effort to rid the world of democracy and yet the Liberal government through actions recently displayed revealed that it was able to accomplish what the Kaiser and Adolf Hitler were unable to accomplish, the destruction of parliamentary democracy in this country.

The army has a separate army welfare fund to look after servicemen who are presently serving, while in the case of the air force the one fund looks after both classes of men.
We have a situation where a fund is not responsible directly to parliament, yet is receiving certain benefits from public moneys, even though indirectly. This is something which bears a close relationship to problems which arise in the Department of Veterans Affairs, and I think there should be a closer contact between these two funds. I should like to think that the minister or his parliamentary assistant, who may be more directly interested in this, would look carefully into this situation.
As the minister knows, during the war large sums of money accumulated in the nonpublic funds accounts in messes and canteens of the air force, and toward the end of the war these were turned over to the air force benevolent fund. Contributions continue to be made to that fund from similar sources in the air force. There is a strong feeling growing up among veterans who served in the air force that they do not have the same opportunity of benefiting from the air force benevolent fund as do the men who are presently serving. In the case of a man presently serving there are officers immediately at hand who are well acquainted with the benefits which are available and applications can be made and recommendations sent forward if the case is a good one, and a grant or loan is usually made. The air force veteran

who is now a civilian feels that he is denied the services of such qualified men, that therefore his case is not so well presented, and as a result the benefits which he receives are not in proportion to the contributions which veterans as a group made during the war.
I think the system adopted in the case of the army benevolent fund is a good one. In that case field services are provided by the Department of Veterans Affairs. I would recommend that the minister look carefully into the situation with regard to the air force benevolent fund to see if a similar arrangement could not be made. I think it is most important that it should be made in the case of the air force, because the proportion of men now serving in the air force as compared with those who served during the war is much greater than in the case of the army. Therefore it is more important, not less, that two separate funds should be set up; an air force welfare fund for serving members of that service, and an air force benevolent fund which would apply only to veterans of the air force.
After all, it was the veterans who in the first case contributed through their nonpublic fund accounts very large amounts of money to the benevolent fund. Toward the end of the war they lost complete control of that as individuals. The non-public funds were turned over to the air force benevolent fund, and in most cases canteens, messes and so on had no alternative but to turn over the profits that had accumulated during the war. I know from experience that in many cases messes operated at a higher profit than they would have if they had anticipated what was going to happen.
It may be said that I have just expressed an opinion or that several veterans of the air force, who tend to grouse anyway, are just complaining because they do not feel they are getting a fair break, but I see a paragraph in the eleventh annual report of the Royal Canadian Air Force benevolent fund which substantiates what I have to say. I have discussed this matter with the commanding officer and with other members of the regiment; I have discussed it with a number of other people concerned in the matter, and I think there is absolutely no question in regard to the facts as I presented them.
The difficulty, as I have indicated before, I think is that there is too narrow an interpretation of section 13 (2). I think the difficulty really stems from the fact that during

Supply-Veterans Affairs the war there was undoubtedly a considerable abuse of military transport, in that it was used for personal purposes of all kinds. Those abuses inevitably continued after the war, and therefore the general position taken by the government has been that people who take military transport and use it in an unauthorized way, if they are injured or killed, are not going to be rewarded, as it were, by the grant of pensions and things of that sort. It is too literal and too strong an application of that general idea. I think it causes the difficulties in these motor accident cases.
In every one of these motor accident cases where injury or death has resulted, that I have known about, it has been extremely difficult to get a pension granted. As I say, I think it stems from that position of contempt for military transport, and of not paying pensions unless it can be proved definitely that it was military transport authorized for use, that it was being used for military duty and so on. It was a correction of what I consider this unjust application of these ideas that I was requesting the minister to look into, particularly as far as this case was concerned.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure the hon. member for Calgary North that, in my remarks addressed to the hon. member for Prince Albert, I was not questioning for one minute the accuracy of the facts which he stated to this house, but simply questioning whether those facts had been properly put before the commission.
I should like, at the beginning of my remarks, to thank all hon. members who have participated in this debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. As is usual and proper, there have been praises for the officials of the department and criticism of the minister and of the policy of the government, and I suppose that is as it should be. However, I might say that I readily accept on behalf of the officials of my department the praises which were expressed of them, because I feel that the veterans' charter is administered and implemented not only with efficiency but in a humanitarian and understanding way. That is done both at headquarters and in the field by officers of the department who are veterans themselves in almost all cases, and I think that might be an explanation of their attitude of mind.
I must say I was particularly glad to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South emphasize the fact that the department does act, that it does things without any special urging or pressure, because as I said in my opening remarks and have said on other


occasions, it is the aim of the government, and it is certainly the aim of the Department of Veterans Affairs, to keep the veterans' charter constantly under review to ensure that it is always up to date and that it is meeting as much as possible the changing needs of veterans and their dependents.
I do not propose to deal at this stage with all the points that have been raised. I think I can do so better on the specific votes as they are called. I think it will be agreed that most of the points raised by way of criticism are matters that have been discussed before in the house, outside the house and before the special committee on veterans affairs. I think that all hon. members will agree that in many instances it is most difficult to draw the line for qualification for benefits under legislation such as that which comprises the veterans' charter. It is difficult, whether the line be one regarding a means test, or service qualification, or one concerning a time limit. In acts such as the War Veterans Allowance Act, the Pension Act and the Veterans' Land Act, no matter where the line is drawn there will always be borderline ones which just fail to qualify and may in fact well be cases of hardship. I think that is true of all legislation of a social character, what might be termed social legislation. It is one of the difficulties that governments meet, whether at the federal, provincial or municipal level.
Most of the hon. members who have spoken up to now on this item have referred at length to the ceilings on permissible income in the War Veterans Allowance Act. I think in the debate on second reading of the bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act last session I submitted at quite some length and to the best of my ability the reasoning of the government in fixing the ceilings at their present levels, that is $840 for a single man and $1,440 for a recipient at the married rate. I pointed out, at the time, that if the ceilings had been established at $1,200 single and $2,000 married, the War Veterans Allowance Act could and would, in a number of cases, be a supplement to normal income.
I also pointed out the necessity of keeping all benefits available to veterans in balance, and that when fixing the ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act cognizance must be taken of the disability pensioner under the Pension Act. I also pointed out that this had always been done throughout the history of veterans' legislation in this country. The present ceiling of $70 a month for a single recipient is equivalent to slightly more than a 55 per cent disability pension, that is, a pension paid for injury incurred in service,

while the ceiling of $120 a month for a married recipient is equivalent to approximately a 70 per cent pension under the Pension Act.
As I said at that time, if the ceiling on the single rate were raised to $1,200 that would be the equivalent of an 80 per cent disability pension. It would be in fact $25 less a month than a 100 per cent disability pension. A ceiling of $2,000 on permissible income at the married rate would be just $40 a year less than a 100 per cent disability pension at married rate. A 100 per cent disability married pensioner gets $2,040 or $170 a month.
The hon. member for Royal said that a disability pensioner with a small pension or a small superannuation allowance is prejudiced because of these permissible ceilings. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that, regardless of where you set the ceiling, a case could be made showing that the ceiling was not fair to certain people. That is what I was pointing out in the earlier part of my remarks when I referred to the difficulties that exist in dealing with such legislation.
For instance, let us say that the ceiling was raised to $1,200 a year for a single man. A war veterans allowance recipient at age 70 would receive $40 by way of old age security payment and $60 war veterans allowance, or the maximum permitted under this $1,200 ceiling. But let us consider the case of a 45 per cent disability pensioner under such circumstances. That the case, for instance, of a man who has lost an eye. I believe that, according to the table of disabilities, the loss of one eye creates a right to a 40 per cent disability pension. Let us say this man is a 45 per cent pensioner, that he has lost one eye and has some gunshot wounds. At age 70 this man would receive $675 under the Pension Act, he would receive $480 under the Old Age Security Act and roughly about $5 a month by way of war veterans allowance, making in all a total of $1,200. I think that this 45 per cent disability pensioner might say, to use the terminology of the hon. member for Royal, that he was prejudiced in that he would be getting very little benefit from his disability pension.
I dealt at much greater length with this question last year and I did note that although hon. members have again made the same representations-I know they do so with the greatest sincerity-no one dealt with the side of the case that I put up last year.
In the course of his remarks one hon. member said this: "It would not cost the government very much more just to raise the ceiling to $1,200 for the single recipient and $2,000 for the married recipient." I wish that were so, Mr. Chairman. However, it 67509-375i
Supply-Veterans Affairs has been estimated-and these estimates are fairly accurate-that to raise the ceiling to those levels, with the present rates being paid, would increase the liability for war veterans allowance which appears in the estimates as $41,192,000 by $13,900,000, which would be, I believe, a little more than a 30 per cent increase in the present liability.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: My hon. friend says it needs checking up again. May I say that I have noticed one thing, and it is this. Every time I have given estimates they have been challenged. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: Why not try being liberal once in a while?

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
I may say that is about the only occasion on which the department is too conservative.
While speaking on this question of raising the allowance may I say there is one point which seems to be forgotten. It has been admitted by hon. members and certainly by veterans' organizations across the country that the changes which were made last year in the formula used for casual earnings had been of considerable help to the veterans under war veterans allowance, and that the

more generous approach which the department had taken in the handling of this legislation had certainly brought about great benefits. But there is one group, and I think they are the ones to whom our attention should be directed particularly, who constitute what might be described as the difficult cases.
I refer to the war veterans allowance recipient who has absolutely no other source of income; who is totally unemployable; who cannot benefit from casual earnings because he is incapable of doing so; who has no disability pension; who has no superannuation. Regardless of the level to which you raise the ceiling on permissible income I submit that you cannot help this man directly, because he has no other source of income. That is where the assistance fund comes in.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: Would there not be one exception, namely the man who is 70 years of age and who would receive old age pension?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
I shall deal with that matter. My hon. friend knows that an unemployable veteran might come in long before he is 60. He might come in under the war veterans allowance if he is totally disabled physically or mentally, and nothing can be done; no matter how high you raise the ceiling, you do not help that man. That is why we created the assistance fund a few years ago.
There is one thing I have noticed, and it is this. Whereas the creation of that fund was discussed at the time, in any representations that are now made to increase the ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act, there is no longer any demand that this assistance fund should disappear. All who are familiar with the operation of the act realize the necessity for it.
I think the hon. member for New Westminster mentioned the rigidity of the formula used in granting assistance under this fund. I did refer to that in my opening remarks. Last year we did broaden the formula used to qualify under the fund, and we did follow very closely its operation during the year. As I mentioned in my opening remarks, in my own estimation there are cases in which the formula now is not flexible enough, and it is the intention of the department and the war veterans allowance board to go into this and be able to deal with those individual cases of hardship which remain even with the existence of the fund.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Royal asked me if the war veterans allowance recipients reaching the age of 70 would not be able to benefit by the full amount of the old age security payment if the ceilings were raised to the levels that have been

suggested. Well, that is quite true. This matter was raised by other members. On other occasions, I have given the government's view on the matter. I know I have been questioned in this house and outside. The tact of the matter is, whether or not one wishes to admit it, that one has to go back some years to the origin of the war veterans allowance to realize just what was behind that legislation. I have said this before the Canadian Legion at their dominion convention, and nobody contradicted me. Nobody has contradicted me so far. I should like, if I may, to quote exactly what I did say at that time, because it explains why certain things that are requested under the War Veterans Allowance Act, in the view of the government cannot be done. These remarks were made in 1954 at Toronto:
War veterans allowances have been based, since their inception in 1930, on the premise that service in a theatre of war preaged a veteran and placed him in a more unfavourable position in the labour market than would have been the case if he had not had such service. Because of this accelerated aging, the allowances were introduced to provide for veterans who needed at age 60, a form of social security not available to their non-veteran contemporaries until they reached the age of 70.
In effect, it was an old age security scheme designed especially to meet conditions peculiar to veterans who had seen combat service.
Now-some of you may object to that assimilation of the war veterans allowance to other social security measures. But the fact remains that a perusal of the debates in the house and the deliberations of the parliamentary committee of 1930 will bear me out on this point.
This being the case, any major changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act-particularly some which have been suggested-cannot help but have serious financial implications in other fields of governmental activities.
Mr. Chairman, that basically is why, when a recipient of war veterans allowance reaches the age of 70, the amount of his allowance is reduced by the amount of the old age security payment he receives. Otherwise, for all practical purposes, he would be receiving the equivalent of two old age pensions coming from two different sources. Unfortunately that is the position and no one has ever denied it. It is impossible to do so if you go back and study the origin of the legislation and the debates that took place at that time.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER

Because the balance of the war veterans allowance within the ceiling is paid to him as assistance on account of his war service. The same reasoning applies to some of the other representations which were made. I do not think it can be ignored.
