The allowance was raised from $50 a month to $60 a month, but the margin was not changed from $10 a month.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: I do not think that comes into it at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: We think it does.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: This is one case where my hon. friend and I differ in our views. However, to return to what I was saying concerning service in England during the first war, it was suggested that it should be recognized as a qualification for war veterans allowance. I think if we go to the origin of this legislation, Mr. Chairman, we have to recognize that eligibility for war veterans allowance is based on service in an actual theatre of war. I know the hon. member for Royal in the course of his remarks the other day said that it used to be like that but it does not exist any more. I would like him to get together with his colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, because in the course of his remarks concerning war veterans allowance recipients he referred to them as "those fighting front line soldiers".

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: That was the original idea. I would like to ask the minister this question in order to see if he and I agree. Is it not true that we give war veterans allowance to men who have dual service, and that a man who only had service in England in the first war and only had service in Canada in the second war without ever being near the front line receives war veterans allowance?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: I also referred to the man who was in the back lines in France and never got near the front. That is my argument on behalf of the men who had service in England. I think we have come a long way from the original idea.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
I do not fully agree with the hon. member for Royal, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the dual service veteran. I think the hon. member is as familiar as I am with the history of that particular section of the War Veterans Allowance Act. This change was brought in originally in 1944, and it was an order in council passed under the authority of the War Measures Act. It was known as the "veterans' dual service pension order". The hon. member will recall that, when we sat in the veterans affairs committee in the years that followed the war and were asked to put in statutory form the various orders that had been passed, something had to be done about that particular pension order and it was added to the War Veterans Allowance Act at that time as part III of the act.
Finally when we reviewed and consolidated the act in 1952-my hon. friend sat as a member of that committee-it was decided that rather than have a separate part of the War Veterans Allowance Act to deal with


the dual service pension order, it would be simply included in the act as a section and it became, I think, section 30. These veterans were described in section 30 of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I say we cannot overlook the fact that the war veterans allowance was originally created and has always been looked upon as legislation designed to deal with the needy veteran who served in an actual theatre of war. It has been said that many of these men stayed in England not because of their own choice. They may have been kept there because they were cn the administrative staff or for some other reason, and mention has been made of the fact that they would have liked to serve in an actual theatre of war. I point out, Mr. Chairman, that is the case with every man who enlists. If service in England during world war I is recognized as a qualification for war veterans allowance I do not see how we could eventually avoid recognizing service in Canada.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: That is not a logical conclusion.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
My hon. friend shakes his
head, but I would point out to him that particularly during the second world war many men stayed in Canada because they were kept here for some reason or another. I would cite, for example, the case of a flying instructor. I know some of them per-sonnally who because they enlisted at the beginning of the war were considered too old to fly, because the air force was pretty choosey concerning age in those days at the beginning of the war. Those men were put on the instruction staff and remained there. They flew in Canada in that capacity throughout the war, and certainly they underwent as great a risk to their lives as anybody who served in England during the first war. If we were to consider preaging and the fact of having undergone hardship being likely to bring about preaging, I know my hon. friend is familiar with some of the training the army, for instance, was put through particularly during the final years of the war. I suggest that at the present time disability pensions are being paid to people who suffered disability on battle drill courses or assault courses where undoubtedly they were put through a very hard type of training.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
They were in the first war,
too.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
I am just mentioning those
cases to illustrate how difficult it would be, if we granted the request that service in England during the first war be recognized, not to include service in Canada, as service in an actual theatre of war.

It was also mentioned that this change would not be very costly. It is estimated that recognizing England as a theatre of war during world war I would cost approximately $7,920,000, which would have to be added to the present cost of war veterans allowance; and of course if this were done and the previous request of some hon. members were granted that the ceilings be raised, this amount would also have to be increased.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
In that connection may I ask
the minister if it is not true that the figure he quoted includes several thousand veterans who arrived in England in 1918, at about the time the war ended, and all the real service they had in England was training in some of the reserve camps?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext: I am afraid it would include all service in England; that is right. It is impossible for me to give the figure concerning those who came in at such a date and so on, but I am giving the figure for 1955. It is estimated that the probable number of veterans living in 1955 who had seen service only in England was 52,000. In arriving at this estimate we assumed that the same proportion would apply for war veterans allowance as in the case of other veterans who qualify, and that would be approximately 23 per cent. This refers to world war I, of course.

subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
These figures were given
last year in the committee on estimates, and I quoted them last year when I was speaking. A total of 52,000 served in England, and the official who gave these figures estimated that 11,500 would be eligible for war veterans allowance, or 22 per cent-the minister makes it 23 per cent-with the cost being $9,650,000. I want to point out that on the basis of the total number of survivors of world war I and taking the number drawing war veterans allowance as being 10 per cent, the figure for the United Kingdom would be reduced greatly, and I estimate it would be only $4,200,000.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COMPARATIVE COSTS OF PRODUCTION OF ELECTRIC POWER
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite an expert on figures and the interpretation of statistics, but I can only give to the committee the views which my officials and the financial members of my staff give to me. Those are based on our past experience with other veterans.
There is another point which was mentioned by some hon. members and to which I should like to refer briefly. This concerns the payment of war veterans allowance to recipients who were living outside of Canada for reasons of health. Last year the hon. member for Kootenay West spoke at some length on this subject and I told him that we
Supply-Veterans Affairs would be looking into these particular cases, which would call for an amendment to the act. Since that time I have had discussions with officials of my department, and I asked them to investigate this situation thoroughly.
I regret to say that, after a great deal of discussion and thought we find it is not feasible to amend section 14 (1) as was suggested. Under the present legislation a recipient may absent himself from Canada for a period of up to three months in any calendar year without affecting the payment of his war veterans allowance, and he may dovetail his stay outside of Canada from one calendar year into another and thus be able to absent himself for six months without having his allowance reduced. However, he can do this only once every two years.
There are serious obstacles to making the suggested change in the legislation, one being the provision of treatment for recipients of war veterans allowance who are living outside of Canada. A great proportion of them need medical treatment from time to time, and this would involve the extension of the provisions of section 12 of the veterans' treatment regulations. It would be most difficult indeed to implement such provisions.
Then there would be the difficulty of arranging for periodical medical examinations of veterans who have not reached the age of 60 years but who are in receipt of war veterans allowance because they are totally unemployable. Such examinations would be most difficult indeed under the circumstances. There would also be the matter of administering the means test in connection with people living outside of Canada. Of course if we followed the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and eliminated the means test that obstacle would disappear, but I am afraid I cannot agree to that suggestion.
Complicated administrative problems would be created where the wife of a recipient of war veterans allowance did not accompany him when he left Canada but remained in Canada. It would be most difficult to amend this section of the act to permit a war veterans allowance recipient to go outside Canada to only one or two specific countries. During the course of the debate last year reference was made to the veteran who might wish to go to the southern part of the United States or Mexico. If the act were opened up to permit the payment of allowances in other parts of the world, the administrative problems thus created would be most complicated.

Supply-Veterans Affairs know how we could deal administratively with veterans in that country. The bronze plaque in the Lancaster military hospital is a very large plaque. I have given the inscription. The plaque measures 36 inches across and is 18 inches in depth. It is very large. One-third of the bronze plaque is taken up with the inscription I have read and to which I have given approval. Two-thirds of the plaque, the larger portion, is taken up with the names of the gentlemen who opened that hospital, a hospital erected by the people of Canada for the veterans of this country. It is to that practice that I raise objection. These hospitals as well as other public buildings have to be opened but those who open them are serving in a temporary capacity and their names do not need to be recorded for all time.
I recognize the fact that the minister is a representative of the new ruling class of Canada, the pseudo-aristocracy, the descendants of the family compact, foreshadowed in section 49 of the British North America Act; nevertheless I do not think it is correct that their names should be recorded for all time on public buildings in Canada. Consequently I draw attention to the fact that this plaque, which may be satisfactory to the people of Lancaster would not be satisfactory,

I think, in the city of Winnipeg, records the fact that the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the then deputy minister of veterans affairs opened that hospital and their names and titles are recorded in bronze, occupying two-thirds of that large plaque and dwarfing the one-third devoted to the inscription recording the fact that the people of Canada erected the hospital for their veterans. The type used for the Minister of Labour is one inch in size for each letter, and for the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his deputy the type is three-quarters of an inch in size for each letter.
If you look at the plaques which were set up just outside the library, on the occasion of the opening of the renovated building, you will see that they are much more modest in character and in the size of the type that is used. But at this veterans hospital erected by the people of Canada for disabled veterans and those in trouble, in great blazing letters three-quarters of an inch in height, we have recorded for all time the names of these temporary occupants of office, two of whom happen to be present here in the House of Commons and the other serving as a deputy minister. I have one question to raise with respect to the war veterans allowance. I am raising it now because, as a matter of fact, this morning I had another letter about this case which reminded me of it. It raises a problem on which I should like the minister to make a brief statement. We know that the war veterans allowance is paid under various categories, over 60 and so on and so forth, permanently unemployable, and then you come down to one who, because of physical or mental disability or insufficiency combined with economic handicaps, is incapable of maintaining himself.
The situation which was brought rather forcibly to my mind this morning by a rather pathetic letter-a situation with which the minister or his departmental officials dealt two years ago and which has now been revised-is one such as this. You have a veteran who has been receiving war veterans allowance. He had a kidney disability, as a result of which one kidney was removed by operation. He had tuberculosis of the other. He had been receiving war veterans allowance up to two years ago, when somebody decided that he was then capable of earning a living. An appeal was taken and as a result the war veterans allowance was restored. Since then he has had two more operations on that kidney, so his condition apparently was not too good two years ago. Now he has been in Camp Hill hospital for examination, and he received a letter last week saying that, according to the doctors, he was now capable of earning a living. So his war veterans allowance has been cancelled as of July 31 this year.
I can understand the position of the department. Apparently, the section is mandatory and provides that if the medical officer says that he is capable of earning a living, there is no alternative. Frankly, I do not know what the minister can do about it. I think there should be some elasticity brought into the picture somewhere. Obviously there has been such elasticity or else he could not have got around the appeal two years ago. When you go on to the next section, you find that it is much more elastic, where provision is made for payment of benefits to employable veterans because there the requirement is that he is unable to maintain himself or is capable of taking only light employment.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
At the same time, I know this is not the place to amend the act, and I quite appreciate the fact that some departmental officials have taken it upon themselves to view that section very leniently in restoring war veterans allowance, and they will have the same responsibility on their shoulders within the next few days. But I would think there should be another section in there which would give some discretion.
The situation is this. This particular man is a labourer with a grade VI education and living away out in the country. I know he was told at one time, "Perhaps you can operate an elevator". He never saw an elevator in his life, and he would be scared to death if he got into one; or if he got into one and operated it, he would probably kill whoever was in it. If he had training as a bookkeeper or as a school teacher, possibly he would be able to earn a living. But as a labourer, living in a rural community where, frankly, the only employment open to a labourer would be that of digging ditches, it is practically impossible for him to earn his living, though from a medical standpoint he might be capable of earning a living if he had employment categories open to him.
I am bringing the matter to the attention of the minister. As I said, I appreciate the fact that on an earlier occasion there was elasticity in the interpretation given to the section, and that was helpful. On many occasions there must be need for such elasticity. But I would think it would be a matter worthy of an amendment of some kind, so the minister or his departmental officials would have discretion there. When you get shall we say a hard-boiled doctor- and some of them are hard-boiled because, I suppose, they are obliged to be so in order to carry out their profession-who says, "You are capable of earning a living, in my opinion", then what does the department do about it?

Despite what the Minister of Veterans Affairs said today in reply to


what I thought were excellent representations made by many members for raising the ceiling on the war veterans allowance, I hope he will give this matter still further consideration. It seems to me that the Legion is most responsible in the figures it has suggested, namely a $1,200 ceiling for single recipients and $2,000 for married recipients. Because those figures are fair and responsible, we on this side of the house naturally do not like to suggest anything less.
However, it seems to me that the minister took advantage of that situation and was satisfied to take the view that there were only two choices; either the present ceiling or the figure advocated by the Canadian Legion and suggested in this house. If the minister and the government have not yet seen the light and are not prepared to go as far as the Legion has suggested I would hope that at least they would realize the force of the argument that has been made in the house and would start moving upward the ceilings on the total incomes of war veterans allowance recipients.
I listened with interest to the arguments the minister advanced today, and I confess that he did not convince me as well as he appears to have convinced himself. He pointed out, for example, that to establish a ceiling of $1,200 on the income of war veterans allowance recipients would be to set a figure equal to about 80 per cent of the disability pension. I point out to him, however, what all of us realize, that to establish a ceiling of $1,200 for single war veterans allowance recipients does not give them $1,200 a year. It merely permits them to supplement their war veterans allowance up to that figure.
May I also point out the other difference that would still obtain between the war veterans allowance recipient, if the ceiling were set at $1,200, and the disability pensioner, namely that there is no ceiling on the income of a disability pensioner. It seems to me that these same answers apply to the other examples the minister gave, and that in fact to establish a higher ceiling on war veterans allowances would not be as unfair-I am not sure if that is the word he used but that is the spirit I caught from what he said-as he suggested it would be to the disability pensioner. I do not hear any disability pensioners complaining about the suggestion that something better be done for war veterans allowance recipients. As a matter of fact those ceilings in the War Veterans Allowance Act have a limiting effect on the income of many recipients of the disability pension.

As the minister and all of us know, where a disability pensioner is receiving an amount as a disability pension which is equal to or higher than the ceiling set in the War Veterans Allowance Act he is denied the possibility of any supplement under the War Veterans Allowance Act. On the other hand, if the ceiling were raised under the War Veterans Allowance Act it would be of assistance not only to those who receive only the war veterans allowance, not only to the others who might come in, but it would be of assistance as well to many who receive disability pensions in the lower percentage brackets.
The minister also gave the example of a war veterans allowance recipient now drawing $60 a month. He said that if the ceiling were raised to $1,200 a year or $100 a month, that would permit him, when he reached 70 years of age, to draw the $40 old age pension in full and still keep the full amount of his war veterans allowance, bringing him up to $100 per month. Against that the minister set the case of a 45 per cent disability pensioner drawing $675 a year disability pension and $480 old age security or a total of $1,155 a year. He said further that that person, if the ceiling were raised to $1,200, would be able to draw only another $45 a year as war veterans allowance.
As I took it from the minister, he seemed to suggest that there was something of an imbalance between the treatment accorded the disability pensioner and the war veterans allowance recipient in that situation. May I point out that so far as the war veterans allowance recipient to whom he referred is concerned, prior to reaching age 70, at $60 a month he is already receiving $720 a year which, of course, is more than the 45 per cent disability pensioner is receiving under that legislation. The 45 per cent disability pensioner does not complain about that so long as there is a margin that permits him to get a supplement by way of war veterans allowance if his income is not adequate.
All told, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that these comparisons the minister sought to make between the position of the disability pensioner and the war veterans allowance recipient are not valid. For these, and for the other excellent reasons that have been advanced in the discussion of these estimates, I hope that further consideration will be given by the government to raising these ceilings. I wish the government would start making some upward move at this session. Certainly the ceilings should be set at nothing less than the figures suggested by the Legion of $1,200 single or $2,000 married, but surely it is possible to make a start in that upward direction at this session.

I think over the years the Canadian Legion have taken a very responsible attitude so far as government legislation is concerned. Their proposals have always been moderate and responsible. I think their proposals today in relation to the war veterans allowance are very modest indeed. They are not asking, though I think they might have reason to ask, that the basic pension itself be increased above the $60 for a single person or $108 for a married couple. The new income ceiling they suggest of $1,200 per year single or $2,000 a year for a person who is married I think is quite low enough.
Today the cost of living is at an all-time high. If such a person could obtain the extra allowable income to reach the $100 a month, that would be little enough to meet the current cost of living. I would like to see, as others have said, a veterans affairs committee established again. I believe that in the past members of that committee have taken a very sympathetic attitude towards the veterans. I believe that if a representative committee of this house were to discuss this question they would bring in a recommendation that would, in large measure, meet the requests of the Canadian Legion.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Royal is not able to be here this evening because of the activities of the research committee, and he asked me to bring up the matter of assistance provided under the war veterans allowance. I note that the amount spent under this vote last year was about $375,000 less than the amount voted. The act provides for fhe payment of $10 per month or $120 per year to completely unemployable old veterans who are receiving war veterans assistance, but it would appear that the average payment is considerably under that amount. I should like to know the average amount paid to these unemployable old veterans. My information is that instead of $120 per year being paid the average is between $60 and $70, or about one-half.
It would appear from the fact that the amount voted last year was considerably underspent that the regulations have been rigorously applied. I submit that this is one group who are probably in about as bad a situation as any group in the Dominion of Canada. These old veterans are completely unemployable and it is impossible for them to supplement their war veterans allowances. In spite of that fact, if my information is correct on the average they get only a little more than half what the legislation provides.
I should like the minister to tell us what was the average amount paid and why the vote was underspent by more than one-third last year?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member will remember that last year we amended the act to increase the ceilings and the rates, and in so doing we brought in additional veterans. It turned out that we had overestimated the number who might qualify for assistance from the fund. Furthermore, by raising the rates some people who might have applied for assistance under the fund did not do so.
In making our estimate this year we went by our experience last year, but from what has happened in April, May and June it would appear that we may have underestimated. As compared with the same months last year the number of applications received in April, May and June this year were 40 per cent higher.
As of March 31, 1956, there were 6,256 recipients who were receiving assistance

from the fund, and of that number 3,070 represented new applications made during the year, the balance being carried over from the previous year. Of the 2,072 veterans receiving allowances on the basis of married rates, 1,574 received $10 per month or more. Out of a total of 272 widows, 232 received $10 per month or more. Of those two groups, 311 received single payments averaging $58 per year.
In the case of those on single rates, out of 1,501 veterans, 756 received $8 per month or more; out of 1,467 widows, 1,158 received $8 per month or more. In that group 560 received average single payments of $42. Out of a total of 2,348 married rate recipients, 2,117 received assistance at the rate of 85 per cent or more. Out of 2,968 recipients, 2,474 received assistance at the rate of 80 per cent or more.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A rapid bit of mental arithmetic would indicate that the figures the minister has given indicate that the average payment was around $7 per month instead of $10. It would seem to me that as the amount involved here is almost negligible considering our general revenues, being $100,000 or something less than that, this is a case where the legislation and the regulations should be applied in the most liberal manner possible.
I see the minister nodding his head in agreement. I hope that in future years these people will be given the maximum amount the law allows, the $10 per month, without too much question being asked; because, as I say, the total amount of money involved is very small. For people who are getting say $60 per month total income plus the amount of this allowance, if they get $10 per month perhaps they can just get by, whereas if they get only $66 or $67 per month it may mean a terrific amount of hardship. It is a question of people on an extraordinarily low total income where every dollar makes a great deal of difference as to whether they merely exist or perhaps exist with one, two or three of the simple pleasures of life.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

So far the minister has not said anything with regard to the case of Stanley Hepworth to which I referred this afternoon. I think it is important, from two points of view, that something definite be done with regard to this case and others of the same nature. I think it is important first of all from the point of view of the reputation of the Department of Veterans Affairs itself, and second from the point of view of the general morale of the Canadian militia and the matter of getting recruits. When you have the situation of a man who served five years overseas and proved his mettle by winning the Military Medal; who served six years in the militia and had an extraordinarily good record; who obeyed the orders of his commanding officer to turn out on a parade and who, as a result of turning out on the parade, lost his life; and when really because of a technicality based on a mischance when he lost his life his widow has been turned down for pension, I think you have a situation which calls into question in the minds of a large number of people the claims which we have heard that our veterans' legislation is

the best in the world. It also discourages people from joining the militia or continuing in the militia.
It seems to me it is just not good enough to leave the situation as it is. This one case which I have mentioned happens to illustrate the matter particularly well, but there have been other cases of the same kind. It is not good enough to leave the situation where it stands. I think the minister owes it to his own department and to the defence department as well as to this house to make some kind of statement in regard to this particular section 13 (2), I believe it is, of the Pension Act, as to what can be done in order to correct what I think is a very unfortunate state of affairs in regard to this particular case as well as cases generally along this line.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This case which my hon. friend mentioned, Mr. Chairman, is one which would come under section 13 (2) of the Pension Act. This is the section which makes provision in respect of military service in peacetime, whether in the regular service or in the militia. It differs in certain respects from service in wartime, but I do not think I need to go into that; he is quite familiar with it.
In the case which the hon. member mentioned this afternoon, I did have a few heated words with the hon. member for Prince Albert, but I think that was mostly the result of a misunderstanding on both our parts. The facts have to be put before the commission. Now, the facts as they were put before the members of the committee by the hon. member I would say were very well put forward. It is impossible for me to pass any judgment on the decision that was rendered without being able to see whether those facts were actually put before the commission. It does happen quite often that on the initial hearing all the facts which would justify the commission in making an award are not put forward. I take it from what my hon. friend said this afternoon that this was the first hearing.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The second hearing is over.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
At any rate, I think he will understand how difficult it is for me to pass any judgment on the case without being able to see the facts that were put forward. In any event, it would be out of order for me to make any remarks about a decision rendered by the pension commission, which is a completely autonomous body where the minister has no discretion whatever to interfere.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
But it does present a problem. I have been informed by the commission that fortunately most of these cases that are brought forward are quite clear-cut. But there are some that are marginal cases, and it is very difficult for people to decide whether a man was or was not on duty. I know of a couple of such cases that have come to my knowledge. As a matter of fact in these cases, the services, particularly in the last year or two, have been most helpful. The chairman and members of the commission have explained to the services how they must protect the interests of their own men by making it clear whether or not the man was on duty. I have known of cases myself in which the adjutant general or the A.A.G., have come up and explained the circumstances of service under which the accident took place, and favourable decisions have been rendered.
Following the consideration of the estimates last year I looked into this particular section. I do not know how the section can be changed unless the principle which exists now is departed from altogether. I do not know how the mere wording of the section could be changed to achieve the purpose which my hon. friend has in mind, because it is a question of the interpretation of the facts by the commission. We may think at times they are wrongly interpreted. Of course one is free to form one's judgment on the matter, but the wording of the section is correct so far as I can see and does afford the protection it was intended to give to those serving members. I would think that the case which my hon. friend has mentioned is possibly a marginal case, and I think it would be very proper for the person concerned to appeal the case.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not believe this is a case, as the minister has indicated, where the facts have not been put forward. I think the facts have been put forward. The difficulty is, as I said, that the decision has been made really on a technicality. It was founded on a mischance. In other words the army transport which was supposed to be provided for the members of this unit to go to this parade had a breakdown. As a result it did not appear and the senior officer on the spot gave instructions or orders that the men who were there would then go in private cars. There happened to be a sufficient number of private cars there owned by these people. They went in those private cars and this man was killed in a private car returning from the parade. Because it was a private car and not a military vehicle and was not on a per diem or mileage basis, the application for pension has been turned down. Really it amounts to that.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
In other words, as I say, it is a technicality based on a mischance. I believe that is the sort of thing that it should be within our capability and within the capability of the department to overcome, to ensure that an injustice is not done. This unfortunate set of circumstances technically left the case outside the provisions of the Pension Act. Really all I am asking is that the minister and the government look into this and if it is necessary pass an order in council or do something else to overcome that particular difficulty.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is the section 13, subsection 2 which has been causing so much difficulty for a number of years. The answer the minister gives is that the pension commission is an independent body. We accept that. When an inquiry is made of the pension commission they say they have to conduct their proceedings and make their decisions in accordance with the act. The act can be changed only by parliament, and the person who should introduce such a change is the minister. Last year in the estimates committee he told us that this section 13 subsection 2 was under consideration. He has now reported that it has been considered and he sees no way in which it can be altered.
The hon. member for Calgary North has raised now a very good example of the weakness of the act as it is interpreted by the pension commission. It is only about four years ago that I raised in this house a somewhat similar case affecting a member of the regular forces who lost his life. Again it was section 13, subsection 2 under which the decision was rendered. When the hon. member for Calgary North was talking about this particular instance, naturally my mind went back to the McAulay case that I raised before the appeal board of the pension commission and spoke about in the House of Commons. The people who suffer under these decisions which the pension commission finds it has to make in accordance with the act are the widows and children. Surely that is not the intention of parliament or the Canadian people.
In both these instances, the one raised by the hon. member for Calgary North and the one I raised four years ago, the men had given first class service overseas. In the case to which I referred the man continued in the regular army back home, and in the case referred to by the hon. member for Calgary North the man continued in the militia. Both men gave continuous service in the interests of the Canadian armed forces. In both cases the widows are now left without assistance; in both cases the men were acting under orders, as we see it, and both the hon. member for Calgary North and I have had some


military experience. In both cases the pension commission found that these accidents were not directly connected with military service. It just does not make sense to us.
I recall in the McAulay case I was informed by a member of the pension commission that the corporal who later was killed should have refused to obey the order of the sergeant who put in his possession the jeep which he drove. When the hon. member for Prince Albert was talking about the Hepworth case that was mentioned earlier I thought the answer might have been given by some member of the commission to the effect that the men should have refused to obey the order of the major, the second in command of the battalion; that they should have said to him, "Sir, we cannot travel to our destination in civilian cars because if we do that we will not be obeying the rules and regulations".
Subordinate ranks simply cannot take stands like that. They have to obey orders, whether the order is given by a sergeant to a corporal, by a major to a lieutenant or by men of other ranks. To people who have served it is just nonsense to suggest that junior ranks can resist orders given by people senior to them.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that section 13(2) will have to be reconsidered by the minister. As the hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned, the Department of Justice might very well be called in to give some advice on the matter, which is becoming a serious problem.
Last year in the estimates committee I asked the chairman of the pensions commission for some figures with regard to the number of applications to the pension commission by former members of the regular forces under section 13(2). He gave figures for a 5-year period from January, 1950, to March, 1955, and these appear at page 578 of the proceedings of the special committee on estimates of last year. In that 5-year period 6,952 cases came before the commission either on first or second hearing or on appeal, and 89 per cent were rejected. That is a very high rejection figure, and all those rejections were under section 13(2).
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that much more serious consideration must be given to this matter. It is intolerable that the burden of these accidental deaths should fall upon the completely innocent widows and children. It must be remembered that the wives permit their husbands to take part in these military activities, and the army and other service authorities urge the married women to permit their husbands to spend two or three nights a week in militia training of this sort. In the regular forces there is a considerable

amount of encouragement given to the married women in order to have their husbands remain in the services.
There is quite a bit of attention paid to the attitude of the women in this connection until the husband is killed in what those of us who have served and others think is the course of his duty; then the Department of National Defence and the Department of Veterans Affairs say, "There is nothing we can do about it under section 13(2). This accident did not arise out of service". They say to the widow, "Although for several years your husband served his country gallantly in war and in peace, we are sorry but we cannot do anything for you now. You may have children. Well, that is not our responsibility, and you must go somewhere else."
I do not think we can much longer tolerate that state of affairs under legislation which is so frequently described here as the best veterans' charter in the world, and so on. If things of this nature continue to be permitted it must certainly be revised if it is to become the best in the world.

Mr. Chairman, the minister was in his seat when I spoke this afternoon, and I believe he gave his usual attention to what I had to say. I wonder if now that this particular item is before us he would care to comment on whether or not we can expect pensions to be awarded regardless of preenlistment disabilities?
I pointed out this afternoon that any cases I had taken up with the department showed that a substantial number of pension applications were turned down by reason of the department discovering that whatever was wrong was caused by a pre-enlistment condition. At the same time, when the veteran was recruited and joined the forces he was given an A-l classification. I wish the minister would comment on that. I realize there has been some improvement in the act over the years, but I believe that when one is taken into the forces and given an A-l classification it should stand for all time.
Perhaps when the minister speaks he will not be able to give us the statistical answer to this question, but I would like to add a question to those which have been asked by the hon. member for Lanark. How many pension applications, let us say during the last year, were turned down on account of a condition of pre-enlistment origin, and what percentage would that be of the total number of applications that were turned down?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I could not give the hon. member at this time the exact number of applications that were turned down on that specific basis. The question of pre-enlistment condition is
Supply-Veterans Affairs dealt with in section 13, subsection 1 (c) of the act. The principle is that no deduction is ever made in the award because of a preenlistment condition where there has been service in a theatre of war, unless prior to enlistment the condition was obvious or recorded on medical examination.
The meaning of the words "recorded on medical examination" appears in section 2, subsection (u) of the Pension Act. That is a definition that was inserted in 1948 at the suggestion of the members of the veterans affairs committee. In order to understand this section properly, one should read the definition of the words "recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment". Subsection (u) reads as follows:
(u)	"recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment'' includes recorded symptoms or findings in,
(i)	medical proceedings for enlistment,
(ii)	official documentation covering any former period of service,
(iii)	the files of the department,
(iv)	compensation board or insurance company records, and
(v)	the records of a hospital, private physician or other medical authority,
where such record refers to the injury or disease resulting in the disability in respect of which the application for pension is made;
As my hon. friend says, this covers considerable ground. It is quite true that some members of the forces-I understand that this occurred more often during the first war than during the second war-were accepted as being in good physical condition and after being discharged from the service developed certain conditions for which a claim for pension was made. When the commission goes back into the army records, it might be found that a man had been hospitalized in 1942 or 1943 for a certain condition. Then going back into hospital records, they might find that, on being questioned as to his medical history upon entering hospital, he had said that when 10 or 15 years of age he had been hospitalized for a certain condition. The commission might get in touch with the doctor who had looked after him at that particular time. The man might not be familiar with what had happened, but when the doctor was contacted it might be discovered that the condition for which the man was claiming was pre-enlistment. This information would not be withheld wilfully by the man when enlisting, as he might not be aware of this condition, but the commission would find that as part of his medical record, and under the statute it could do nothing but take it into consideration.

speechtext: 1 can assure my hon. friend that if the examinations made prior to enlistment were as thorough as we would like to believe they were, the commission would be saved a lot of trouble. subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Further to what the hon. member for Macleod has said, I should like to pursue this matter a little. I have in my hands the particulars of a case where a man claims that upon enlistment he was found to be in category A. After enlistment he was re-examined four times and always found to be in category A. The man enlisted on May 19, 1941, and left the service on June 3, 1942. He was discharged at that time for medical reasons but was denied full pension benefits because it was claimed that the medical reasons for his discharge had existed prior to enlistment.
I find this a little hard to swallow. We are willing to send a man over the hill, as it were, upon the basis of one medical examination, provided he is declared to be in category A. If we are willing to risk a man's life on the basis of one physical examination he should receive the proper consideration. Former students of mine lost their lives after having had only one medical examination, yet here is a case where a man was declared five times to be in category A.
I notice that in replying to the hon. member for Macleod the minister qualified his statement by saying that a pension decision was partly dependent upon where the service had been. I think that is a most despicable arrangement if such an arrangement exists. Once a man volunteers his life on behalf of the nation he should receive equal treatment regardless of the disposition that is made of that man by the armed forces.


I should like to read from the report of the pensions advocate concerning this man, as follows:
Service documents record treatment for the above noted condition during service. During treatment he stated he had had many colds in his head and pleurisy at eight or nine years of age.
May I just interrupt here. I wonder if this man had asked for exemption from military service on the basis of having had this condition when eight or nine years of age how far he would have got. He would not have got to first base, especially after having five medical examinations which listed him as being in category A. I continue:
According to specialist's report, on 14-4-42, man gave a history that he saw Dr. Campbell Brown in Vernon, B.C., because of frequent colds in chest with cough. On the record this condition existed pre-enlistment with some aggravation during service, but there is no evidence to show that such aggravation arose out of or was directly connected with military service.
I must interrupt to say again that this man was found to be in category A in five examinations. I continue with the report:
The commission rules chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis pre-enlistment condition, aggravated during service in Canada but not pensionable under section 11 (2) as the aggravation did not arise out of nor was it directly connected with military service.
I feel the minister must agree that this is a most niggardly attitude to take when we are willing to shove men over the hill upon the basis of one report which lists them in category A; yet when after five listings in A category these men are thrown out of the service, even against their will, and declared medically unfit and they apply for a pension, we say, "We have now discovered, because of the statement the man made in all honesty at the time of his enlistment, that he had a cold when he was a child, and we therefore find that the disability is of pre-enlistment origin." I think that is disgraceful.

subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I feel I must rise to join with others who are discussing the situation of veterans who, after entering military service and getting a clean bill of health, then have disabilities and find, perhaps after demobilization or discharge, that they are not eligible for pension. It is not my intention at this time to go fully into the case I have had before the department for some three years, but I feel that since other hon. members have spoken on this very issue, I too must make mention of it.
In the case of the veteran of whom I am speaking, he was examined by six specialists of the department on enlistment. He was a first war veteran, having served some three and a half years, and he enlisted for second war service. His category on enlistment for

second war service was Al; he came out P5. He was not demobilized but discharged with the lowest possible category. As I understand it, the terms of the veterans' act are that a veteran is entitled on discharge to be boarded for a medical examination. This man was not boarded for a medical examination, and the determination of his disabilities was not made until 1949. When they were found it was established that he had a heart condition. I have a letter, which is before the department, confirming that he at least feels that his disability was due to service, and the symptoms were those he was boarded for health reasons during his service.
In spite of the fact that many of us bring veterans' cases before the department in which we obtain good consideration and fair and just settlements, it seems to me that in this particular case, where a veteran has served with distinction and has come out with such a low category and there is an establishment of a severe disability, it is up to the pension commission to grant such a veteran some reasonable pension. I want to say to the minister that I intend to fight this case until I get some pension for him that will be in conformity with his service and his disability.
I do not think we can be satisfied with a situation in which a man, having served his country for 10J- years, should be treated in such a way. He was not demobilized but was discharged. As a matter of fact this particular veteran was kept on the staff here in Ottawa for six months after demobilization because the department could not do without his services. To turn him out and to leave the onus of proof on him is completely incompatible with the act, I think, and certainly with simple justice. So I just want to inform the minister that I hope in the near future there will be an easement on the part of the pension commission so the veterans in these cases coming before them will not have the onus of proof put on their shoulders when they cannot establish the exact date when their disabilities occurred. If the veteran has five or six medicals on enlistment, comes out in a P5 category, and is discharged on that account, surely he should be entitled to a decent pension.
So I hope we members of the opposition will not have to get up again and plead with the minister of this department for an easement and an adjustment on behalf of these servicemen. I hope we shall have some justice and that they will receive pensions when they come out with such a low category.

We have had two specimen cases described tonight.

It seems to me that it would be flimsy evidence for the board to accept, that at eight years of age he was subject to colds. Surely the man should receive the benefit of the doubt. I do not think any medical man could ascribe a condition where a man of say 21 was passed fit, as this man was four times, as the hon. member said, and then go away back into his childhood days and make a statement, as he made, that at eight years of age he was subject to colds. What concerns me, having had some part in framing the first part of the legislation, is that that should be fitted in with the other clause in the Pension Act known as the benefit of the doubt clause. speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources includes five branches that deal with widely divergent subjects. The national parks branch administers the national parks of Canada, the national historic parks and historic sites, the Canadian wildlife service and the national museum. The water resources branch is responsible for the federal aspects of water resource questions in Canada. The northern administration and lands branch handles the administration of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory in all its aspects. It is responsible for the administration of Eskimo affairs and also for a great many land problems including the natural resources of the two territories. The forestry branch deals with forest research, forest products research, and forestry management, including agreements with the provinces on forest inventories and reforestation. The Canadian government travel bureau deals with travel promotion and the tourist industry in so far as they are of concern to the federal government.
With this great variety of operations I do not think it would be desirable for me to try to give a comprehensive survey of the work of the department in detail at this time. Such a survey was given when the estimates of my department were before the committee on estimates during last session, and many hon. members will be familiar with the discussion at that time. In all the circumstances I think it may be more satisfactory to deal with a few of the highlights of departmental operations as reflected in the estimates for the coming year. I would wish also to outline in some detail the policy of the department with regard to national parks. When each individual branch is under consideration I shall, of course, be very happy to deal in detail with particular aspects of the work in which any hon. members might be interested.
A principal point of interest in the estimates of any department is always the extent of and the reasons for any major changes from the preceding year. For 1956-57 the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources show an increase of $5,918,662 in the main estimates, plus an additional $3,084,078 in the supplementary

estimates. This makes a total increase of $9,002,740. The increase, as a percentage of the estimates for 1955-56 is quite substantial, approximately 30 per cent. It is my hope that the house will feel that this increase is entirely justified, in fact I would venture to say more than justified, because of the reasons that lie behind the increases where they occur. The actual increases are in fact concentrated in a very few major aspects of operation, and these aspects reflect the places in which the government feels that substantial increases in activity are necessary.
The largest single increase is in the appropriation for the construction of trunk highways and bridges in the national parks. This increase amounts to $4,687,450, including the main and supplementary estimates. There are over 500 miles of main highways in the various national parks. This does not include those portions of the trans-Canada highway that are in the parks, nor does it include minor roads and trails.
These main highways include such important roads as the Banff-Jasper highway; the Banff-Windermere highway; the highways north and south through Prince Albert national park and Riding Mountain national park; the highway connecting with the provincial highways in Fundy national park; the Cabot trail in Cape Breton Highlands national park; and the Ocean View highway in Prince Edward Island national park.
The traffic on these roads has been increasing very markedly in the last few years. The extent and rate of the increase in traffic has now gone far beyond the standards to which most of these highways were built. In virtually all cases extensive or complete reconstruction is becoming necessary. I might also mention that we have found, particularly in the mountain parks, that it is very poor economy to build roads that are below the standard that is required for the wear and tear that the traffic imposes on them. The government, accordingly, has approved a six-year program for the reconstruction of the major park roads.
The total program over the six years will, it is presently estimated, amount to over $60 million. The increase in 1956-57 represents the first instalment of this new program. It includes major construction activity on the Banff-Windermere highway; the Banff-Jasper highway, the Cabot trail, and the Ocean View highway. The program in succeeding years will, on the average, be somewhat greater than the level indicated in this year's estimates.
Other capital items in the parks constitute an increase of $849,118. Accordingly, of
67509-376i
Supply-Northern Affairs the total departmental increase I have mentioned, no less than $5,529,568 is made up by construction and other capital items in the national parks.
The next largest item of increase also reflects an expansion of activity as a result of decisions of policy. This increase is in capital items in the north. One of the major requirements in the Northwest Territories is to provide the kind of educational facilities that will equip the Indian and Eskimo children there for the change that is now taking place at an increasingly rapid rate from their native hunting and trapping economy to an economy based on our way of life. This is not a change, at least in the rate it is taking place, that has been particularly sought or worked for at this time. I dealt in more detail with this matter in the statement on education policy that I made before the committee on estimates last year and I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to go into it at length now.
I might say, however, that the present change is a change that is inevitable because of two interrelated forces. One is the very great increase in economic, defence and other activity in the north that is bringing our way of life inevitably into contact with the native way of life. The other is the fact that the hunting and trapping economy is rapidly becoming less capable of supporting the increasing population. Unless a very serious human problem is to be faced in a few years, extensive education and training of the native people to face a new form of life is urgently required. The largest single increase in northern administration is to provide educational facilities, housing and related administrative facilities in the Northwest Territories. It amounts to $1,821,565, of which educational facilities alone form by far the largest part.
The other substantial aspect of increase in northern administration reflects the policy of the government to stimulate and encourage economic development in the north. The increase for the construction of roads and bridges amounts to $441,830. The increase in funds provided for the construction of the new Aklavik as a centre for administration, education, and welfare in the far north amounts to $1,013,650. These three capital figures are subject to an adjustment downward of $1 million, which was the original estimate of likely short-fall in northern operations, and which has been partly restored in the supplementary estimates. The net result is that the increase of a capital character in our northern administration amounts in total, including the main and supplementary estimates, to $2,277,045.
As hon. members will see from what I have said, the total departmental increase is made

Supply-Northern Affairs up to the extent of $7,806,613 by capital items in the national parks and the two northern territories.
The other substantial increase in the departmental appropriations again reflects a capital item. For a number of years the government has been providing an annual grant to the pulp and paper research institute to assist in the financing of research that is of value to this very important part of the Canadian forest industry. As was announced some months ago, it has now been agreed with the institute that it would be preferable for the government to provide a building of the most modern and efficient character in which research can be carried on and to discontinue the annual grants. There is, therefore, in the estimates an amount of $1,075,000 for a new laboratory to be constructed in Montreal. The total costs of the lab with equipment, to be financed by the federal government, will amount to $2,250,000 over a two-year period.
I think the above summary sets forth virtually all the substantial increases in the appropriations that are now being sought. The capital figures I have mentioned account for increases of $8,881,613. There are minor increases and some decreases in other places which bring the total departmental increase to the figure I gave at the beginning of my remarks, $9,002,740.
There is one other highlight of departmental activity that I should like to mention. As hon. members are aware, water problems have for some time been of concern in the province of Manitoba. As a result of discussions with Premier Campbell, I signed an agreement with him on July 5 for the establishment of a lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba

board. The board will consist of representatives of the province and of the federal government, and its duties will be to-and I quote from the agreement-
. . . plan, supervise and carry out a study of lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba and the resources of water within Manitoba flowing into and from those lakes.
It is to report on:
. . . what further developments and controls of these water resources in its judgment would appear to be physically practicable with particular reference to (a) flood control; and (b) hydroelectric power.
The federal government and the province are sharing equally in the cost of the survey and report.
Mr. Chairman, as I said at the beginning of my remarks I had intended to go on for some time in outlining the policy of the department regarding national parks, but since it is two minutes before ten o'clock I might call it ten o'clock at this time.
